# analytical-dashboard.mdx

Source: https://github.com/jpmorganchase/salt-ds/blob/main/site/docs/patterns/analytical-dashboard.mdx

title: Analytical dashboard
description: "An analytical dashboard enables users to analyze trends, patterns and metrics effectively. You can use this to present data in a hierarchical and intuitive manner.\n\nThe mock-ups displayed in this pattern are available as [templates](https://www.figma.com/file/O3FYUQYXLosmEuZc0T30Qo/Analytical-Dashboard-Pattern?type=design&node-id=1288-5747&mode=design&t=Pu46NKEwCeMRSjPD-0) in Figma _(J.P. Morgan employees only)_."
layout: DetailPattern
tags:
  - pattern
aliases:
  - /salt/patterns/dashboards/analytical-dashboard
  resources:
    [
      {
        href: "https://www.figma.com/file/O3FYUQYXLosmEuZc0T30Qo/Analytical-Dashboard-Pattern?type=design&node-id=1270-11314&mode=design&t=mek99qYi5z5Sxi8J-0",
        label: "Templates",
        internal: true,
      },
    ]
  components: ["Border layout", "Flow layout", "Stack layout", "Tabs"]

<ImageSwitcher
  images={[
    {
      src: "/img/patterns/dashboards/analytical-dashboard/hero_shot_light.png",
      alt: "Example showing an analytical dashboard",
    },
    {
      src: "/img/patterns/dashboards/analytical-dashboard/hero_shot_dark.png",
      alt: "Example showing an analytical dashboard",
    },
  ]}
  label="Dark mode"
/>

## When to use

Use an analytical dashboard to visually represent data that provide insights and analysis of key metrics and performance indicators. Combine various data sources and present information in a concise and interactive format using charts, graphs, tables and other visual elements.

Using an analytical dashboard helps present complex data in a visually organized and intuitive manner, enabling users to view and analyze trends, patterns and metrics effectively. This is useful where data-driven decision making is crucial, such as:

- Data-intensive environments.
- Performance tracking.
- Risk assessment.
- Investment analysis.
- Client reporting.

## How to build

### Anatomy

Creating an analytical dashboard user interface involves a careful consideration of layout features and components to maintain an effective visual hierarchy.

1. **Data visualization widgets**: These include interactive data visualizations such as charts (line charts, bar charts, pie charts, etc.), graphs, heat maps, scatter plots and more. These widgets are usually within a [`Card` component](/salt/components/card) and should effectively represent the data and provide users with insights at a glance.
2. **Filters and controls**: Implement filters and controls that allow users to interact with the data and customize their views. Common examples include date range selectors, dropdown menus, checkboxes and search bars.
3. **Metrics**: Highlight important metrics and key performance indicators (KPIs) that users need to monitor regularly. You can display these as numerical values, gauges or progress bars.
4. **Buttons/icons**: Allow users to export data and reports in various formats (e.g., CSV, PDF) and provide options to share the dashboard with others.

Other features typically found in an analytical dashboard include:

- **Data grid**: Provide tabular views of data for more detailed analysis. Allow users to sort, search and paginate through the data efficiently.
- **Tooltip**: Offer the ability to drill down into more granular data from summary views and view additional information. Users should have access to specific data points and their underlying details.
- **Text**: Clearly display information about the data sources, update frequency and any disclaimers related to data accuracy.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/dashboards/analytical-dashboard/dashboard_anatomy.png"
  alt="Dashboard anatomy"
  border
/>

### Dashboard layout

Ensure that the dashboard is responsive and can adapt to different viewport sizes and devices. Salt provides layout grids as a starting point for designing any user interface that achieves effective alignment and consistency for your dashboard design. View the [Salt Layout Grid library](<https://www.figma.com/file/Qun1kdSvMhq3gk9Bo6dOrC/Salt%3A-Layout-Grid-(Community)?type=design&node-id=16-3068&mode=design&t=l9ZRR3WVCS4BuHZA-0>) for grid templates across different densities.

The following examples use a desktop screen size of 1440 x 1024px and a large, eight-column grid in medium density. The gutters and margins for Salt layout grids are `--salt-spacing-300` across all densities.

- [`BorderLayout`](/salt/components/layouts/border-layout): Use the border layout component to manage the top-level layout of the dashboard, including header, footer and navigation panel elements.
- [`FlowLayout`](/salt/components/layouts/flow-layout): Use for small-scale layouts that require components (such as cards) to be displayed in a responsive row.
- [`StackLayout`](/salt/components/layouts/stack-layout): Use for small-scale layouts that require displaying components in a single row or column and may benefit from the supported visual separators.
- [`Tabs`](/salt/components/tabs): Use to organize and categorize dashboard widgets into local groupings. You can also organize content into multiple dashboards using tabs, each focusing on a specific aspect or topic. This keeps the interface clean and prevents overwhelming users with too much information.
- [`GridLayout`](/salt/components/layouts/grid-layout): Use to manage the layout and responsiveness of the main content area in your dashboard.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/dashboards/analytical-dashboard/dashboard_layout.png"
  alt="Dashboard layout"
  border
/>

Use the F-shaped pattern to guide the user’s focus through the most important widgets on the dashboard. This supports efficient discoverability of elements such as the dashboard’s global controls.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/dashboards/analytical-dashboard/f-pattern_reading_order.png"
  alt="F-Pattern reading order"
  border
/>

When considering the visual hierarchy of an analytical dashboard, ensure the most important widgets on the page draw the user's attention. This varies per dashboard but can include the following:

1. Header
2. Key metrics
3. Charts and graphs
4. Data grids or tables

<GuidanceCallout type="positive" customPillText="Best practices">

- Use [`Drawer`](/salt/components/drawer) to display an expandable panel
  overlaid above a region of your dashboard rather than embedded within the
  existing layout. Users can view additional content without going to a
  different screen.
- Persistently displayed panels should use the west region
  of the border layout instead of a drawer, which can hinder the dashboard user
  experience by hiding key interactive components.

</GuidanceCallout>

### Partially aligned layout

In a partially aligned layout, the main body of the dashboard aligns to a layout grid and combines with surrounding fixed-width panels.

If your dashboard is responsive, the main body region will dynamically resize at different breakpoints. The fixed panel remains the same when the user resizes the viewport, but you can set it to the width of your choice based on desired outcome. Consider the different content types, density and target screen size when making your decision.

<ImageSwitcher
  images={[
    {
      src: "/img/patterns/dashboards/analytical-dashboard/dashboard_partially_aligned.png",
      alt: "Partially aligned dashboard without layout grid in main body region",
    },
    {
      src: "/img/patterns/dashboards/analytical-dashboard/dashboard_partially_aligned_layout_grid.png",
      alt: "Partially aligned dashboard with layout grid in main body region",
    },
  ]}
  label="Layout grid"
/>

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/dashboards/analytical-dashboard/responsive_main_body.png"
  alt="Example showing a responsive main body"
  border
/>

### Fully aligned layout

In a fully aligned layout, the main body of the dashboard and surrounding panels all align to a layout grid.

If your experience is responsive, use the underlying layout grid to set a minimum width for your surrounding panels and adjust your content area based on your predefined breakpoints.

If your experience has a fixed resolution (i.e., isn’t responsive), users can continue to use a layout grid to design consistent layouts.

In the following example, the panel width aligns to the first two columns of the underlying layout grid.

<ImageSwitcher
  images={[
    {
      src: "/img/patterns/dashboards/analytical-dashboard/dashboard_fully_aligned.png",
      alt: "Fully aligned dashboard without layout grid",
    },
    {
      src: "/img/patterns/dashboards/analytical-dashboard/dashboard_fully_aligned_layout_grid.png",
      alt: "Fully aligned dashboard with layout grid",
    },
  ]}
  label="Layout grid"
/>

## Dashboard regions

From a high-level overview, the main content regions of an analytical dashboard are:

- Main body region
- Header region
- Fixed panels

<ImageSwitcher
  images={[
    {
      src: "/img/patterns/dashboards/analytical-dashboard/dashboard_regions.png",
      alt: "Dashboard regions",
    },
    {
      src: "/img/patterns/dashboards/analytical-dashboard/dashboard_regions_breakdown.png",
      alt: "Dashboard regions with visual hierarchy breakdown",
    },
  ]}
  label="Visual hierarchy breakdown"
  caption="Dashboard regions."
/>

### Main body region

The main body region contains dashboard modules/widgets and their content.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/dashboards/analytical-dashboard/main_body_region.png"
  alt="Main body region"
  border
  caption="The main body region of the dashboard."
/>

### Header region

The dashboard header sits at the top of the dashboard body, and its content can be flexible in use. For example, a header can introduce the context of the dashboard, contain information about the latest dashboard update or display personalized user information.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/dashboards/analytical-dashboard/dashboard_header.png"
  alt="Dashboard header"
  border
  caption="The header region of the dashboard."
/>

### Fixed panel

The fixed panel typically contains functionality for user actions that need to be easily accessible. This varies per dashboard but can include components such as filters, toggles and controls. These allow the user to manage the data displayed within the main body or go to multiple dashboard pages.

You can place fixed panels vertically or horizontally within a dashboard, depending on the context.

The below example displays a fixed panel to the left-hand side.

You can use a fixed panel to:

- Accommodate for extensive functionality or a limited amount of user actions, such as search and/or filtering.
- Contain buttons that link to multiple pages in a dashboard.

<ImageSwitcher
  images={[
    {
      src: "/img/patterns/dashboards/analytical-dashboard/fixed_panel.png",
      alt: "Fixed panel",
    },
    {
      src: "/img/patterns/dashboards/analytical-dashboard/fixed_panel_with_spacing.png",
      alt: "Fixed panel with spacing",
    },
  ]}
  label="Content spacing"
  caption="A fixed panel with and without spacing."
/>

#### Width

- The width of a fixed panel depends on the content within it. As a general rule, size the width of the panel to a grid depending on the size of the interactive elements within.

#### Content spacing

- Generally, we recommend driving the content spacing by following the spacing baked into Salt components and applying `--salt-spacing-300` between elements as the default spacing in the chosen density. Tighten as required for more condensed areas.
- Use the [spacing foundation](/salt/foundations/spacing) for further guidance on how to apply spacing.

#### Scrolling

- Fixed panels should remain fixed in position while scrolling the dashboard.

### Content modules

Use [`Card`](/salt/components/card) as a container or widget type to position and convey forms of data, such as charts and grids, within the main body of the dashboard. You can easily arrange and manipulate cards—they're a good choice for a responsive design as you can easily scale them.

<ImageSwitcher
  images={[
    {
      src: "/img/patterns/dashboards/analytical-dashboard/content_modules.png",
      alt: "Content modules",
    },
    {
      src: "/img/patterns/dashboards/analytical-dashboard/content_modules_with_spacing.png",
      alt: "Content modules with spacing",
    },
  ]}
  label="Content spacing"
  caption="Cards are a good choice for enabling responsive design."
/>

<GuidanceCallout type="positive" customPillText="Best practices">
  Keep the content layout within individual cards as consistent as possible
  across the dashboard. This supports scalability, especially if main components
  anchor to familiar locations within a card.
</GuidanceCallout>

#### Layout and style

- We recommend you style cards with the `--salt-container-primary-background` token, and the application with the `--salt-container-secondary-background` token. This is the most effective way to present data, as it provides the highest contrast between visualizations and their immediate backgrounds.
- _(J.P. Morgan employees only)_ For styling data visualizations such as charts, follow the UITK guidelines on data visualization, where you can find further information on presenting data in a visually cohesive manner. We recommend using the categorical color palette within your dashboard design, as it’s ideal for visualizing distinct groups of items.
- As default, use `--salt-spacing-300` between content modules such as cards to promote readability.
- The default padding between modules is `spacing-300`. Depending on the needs and business context of the dashboard, you can change this spacing token if your dashboard needs to display more or less content. View the [spacing foundation](/salt/foundations/spacing) for further guidance.
- Group contextually related content together where possible.
- Order modules from level of priority—which data would the dashboard user consider to be primary vs. secondary?

#### Alternative card layouts

Depending on the amount of data that the user needs to see at once, you can arrange content modules in various layouts alongside common dashboard features, such as fixed panels and key metrics. However, it’s important to not overwhelm users with data; otherwise, it will be hard for them to focus and get a clear overview.

Use the flexibility of the columns in a layout grid to split and arrange cards in various horizontal alignments.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/dashboards/analytical-dashboard/alternative_card_layouts.png"
  alt="Alternative card layouts"
  border
  caption="Alternative card layouts in action."
/>

### Key metrics

A metrics bar is a common example of a dashboard module. It’s a flexible structural attribute that allows highlighting broader level metrics to help provide the user with additional context. It's often positioned horizontally higher up on a dashboard to further emphasize the metrics' importance.

Metric bars should remain clean and concise to provide a higher level oversight of information. Try to adhere to the [Law of Proximity](https://lawsofux.com/law-of-proximity/) and avoid overloading this space with excessive information. Aim for no more than 3–6 key metrics on display, and group contextually related metrics together where possible.

<ImageSwitcher
  images={[
    {
      src: "/img/patterns/dashboards/analytical-dashboard/key_metrics.png",
      alt: "Key metrics",
    },
    {
      src: "/img/patterns/dashboards/analytical-dashboard/key_metrics_with_spacing.png",
      alt: "Key metrics with spacing",
    },
  ]}
  label="Content spacing"
  caption="A metrics bar within a dashboard."
/>

#### Spacing

- Position key metrics in a horizontal layout and apply vertical `--salt-spacing-300` between them to promote readability.
- Use a horizontal container spanning the width of the main body of the dashboard to evenly space out and position a set number of metrics.
- Layout is flexible depending on the dashboard grid. A metrics bar can span the full width of a dashboard (e.g., over 12 columns) or follow a [`SplitLayout`](/salt/components/layouts/split-layout) using the remaining number of available columns across the main body of the dashboard. Use the [`StackLayout`](/salt/components/layouts/stack-layout) or [`FlowLayout`](/salt/components/layouts/flow-layout) components to organize the layout within a metric bar depending on whether metrics should wrap or scroll within a module.

:fragment{src="./fragments/feedback.mdx"}

# announcement-dialog.mdx

Source: https://github.com/jpmorganchase/salt-ds/blob/main/site/docs/patterns/announcement-dialog.mdx

title: Announcement dialog
description: "An announcement dialog promotes new features and can provide users with access to onward action, such as installing version updates."
layout: DetailPattern
tags:
  - pattern
aliases:
  - /salt/patterns/announcement-dialog
  resources:
    [
      { href: "https://storybook.saltdesignsystem.com/?path=/story/patterns-announcement-dialog", label: "Examples" }
    ]
  components: ["Dialog", "Header block", "Button bar"]

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/announcement-dialog/announcement-dialog.png"
  srcDark="/img/patterns/announcement-dialog/announcement-dialog-dark.png"
  alt="Basic announcement dialog"
  border
/>

## When to use

Use an announcement dialog to focus the user's attention on new product features or the highlights of a recent release with a follow-up action, such as **Download update** or **Upgrade**. They can also be used to display a notification that doesn't require a response from the user, such as a welcome message for new users or an upcoming site-maintenance notification.

## How to build

### Anatomy

An announcement dialog comprises of the following components:

1. **Pre-header**: optional labels that can be used to display the product name, announcement type, or a common descriptor when there are multiple announcements.
2. **Heading**: serves as the main title of the announcement.
3. **Content area**: provides additional information or context to the announcement.
4. **Image**: an image of the new feature or visual elements that add appeal and clarity to important messages.
5. **Button bar**: possible actions for users to take.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/announcement-dialog/anatomy.png"
  srcDark="/img/patterns/announcement-dialog/anatomy-dark.png"
  alt="Announcement dialog anatomy"
  border
/>

### Layout

- Use the [Header block](/salt/patterns/header-block) to display a header and pre-header.
- Use the [Dialog](/salt/components/dialog) and it's components as the base structure of the announcement dialog.
- Use a [Button bar](/salt/patterns/button-bar) to display any actions at the bottom of the dialog. See the button bar pattern to understand how to implement actionable interactions within dialogs across your applications.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/announcement-dialog/spacing.png"
  srcDark="/img/patterns/announcement-dialog/spacing-dark.png"
  alt="Announcement dialog spacing and layout"
  border
/>

## Multi-announcement dialog

If there are multiple features that need to be announced, include a progress label showing the current and total number of slides in the button bar. The slide indicator uses `--salt-spacing-200` from the core buttons.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/announcement-dialog/multi-slide.png"
  srcDark="/img/patterns/announcement-dialog/multi-slide-dark.png"
  alt="Announcement dialog with multiple announcements"
  border
/>

## Full image

If your announcement would benefit from a large image, vertically stack the content area and image. Apply `--salt-spacing-300` between announcement description and image.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/announcement-dialog/full-image.png"
  srcDark="/img/patterns/announcement-dialog/full-image-dark.png"
  alt="Announcement dialog with a stacking full image and content area"
  border
/>

## Content area scrolling

In most cases, scrolling shouldn't be required. If additional content does exceed the available space, only the content area and image should scroll together—keeping the header and button bar visible at all times.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/announcement-dialog/scrolling.png"
  srcDark="/img/patterns/announcement-dialog/scrolling-dark.png"
  alt="Announcement dialog with content area and image scroll"
  border
/>

<Callout
  status="success"
  title="Best practices"
>
- The content in the announcement description should be short and concise. This allows users to quickly grasp the necessary information, reducing cognitive load and preventing abandonment.
- By default, the entire image or infographics should be visible without scrolling. To achieve this, adjust the size of the dialog or check that the image is appropriately cropped.
</Callout>

## Responsive behavior

Once the announcement dialog hits a certain breakpoint, you can configure the layout to either:

1. Stack the announcement description and image.
2. Change the orientation to stack the button bar.

### Stacked content area

This mirrors the full image dialog mentioned above.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/announcement-dialog/stacked-content.png"
  srcDark="/img/patterns/announcement-dialog/stacked-content-dark.png"
  alt="Announcement dialog with a stacked content area"
  border
/>

### Stacked button bar

Refer to the [stacked button bar](/salt/patterns/button-bar#stacked-button-bar) guidance for more information. For a multi-announcement dialog, the progress label appears above the buttons. 

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/announcement-dialog/stacked-button.png"
  srcDark="/img/patterns/announcement-dialog/stacked-button-dark.png"
  alt="Announcement dialog with a stacked button bar"
  border
/>

# app-header.mdx

Source: https://github.com/jpmorganchase/salt-ds/blob/main/site/docs/patterns/app-header.mdx

title: App header
description: "An app header is a consistently available element that sits at the top of every application interface. It contains a brand logo or mark and application-wide functionality, including navigation and utility actions."
layout: DetailPattern
tags:
  - pattern
aliases:
  - /salt/patterns/app-header
  resources:
    [
      { href: "https://storybook.saltdesignsystem.com/?path=/story/patterns-app-header--app-header", label: "Examples"},
    ]
  components: ["Navigation item", "Button"]
  relatedPatterns: ["Navigation", "Vertical navigation"]

  <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/app-header/app-header-hero.png"
    alt="App header example"
    border
  />

## When to use

Use as the primary element to orient users within the UI. The app header should be globally persistent, enabling easy navigation and access to utilities.

## How to build

### Anatomy

The app header has three functional areas:

1. **Branding:** Displays a brand logo or mark followed by the application name in text form. This should always link to the product’s homepage.
2. **Navigation:** Serves as the container for the primary navigation. Its inclusion is optional if you have single-page applications or use a persistent side navigation.
3. **Utilities:** Provides access to persistent application-wide utilities, such as external links, search, notifications, help, account details and settings.

  <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/app-header/app-header-anatomy.png"
    alt="Header functional areas—branding, navigation and utilities."
    border
  />

### Desktop layout

- Use [`NavigationItem`](/salt/components/navigation-item) to build the horizontal page navigation, as explained in the [navigation pattern](./navigation).
- Use `FlexLayout` with justify set to `space-between` to position the brand logo, navigation and utilities.

  <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/app-header/app-header-layout.png"
    alt="Example showing header’s desktop layout construction."
    border
  />

### Mobile layout

- Use a [stack layout](/salt/components/layouts/stack-layout) with the direction property set to row to position the menu button and the logo. 
- The menu button opens and closes the navigation [drawer](/salt/components/drawer). 
- Use a stack layout to position the [vertical navigation](./vertical-navigation) and utilities within the drawer.

  <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/app-header/app-header-mobile-layout.png"
    alt="Example showing header’s mobile layout construction."
    border
  />

### Logo treatment

Always place your logo on the top-left corner of the application. It can be preceded by the app name in text form as part of the branding area. This area can vary in size and composition where:

- The max-height follows the fixed default height for base components in each density —size-base.    
- The width responds to its content —standalone logo; or logo & app name together. 

Refer to the [J.P. Morgan Brand Toolbox](https://www.jpmcbrandtoolbox.com/users/sign_in) brand guidelines if using an authorized J.P. Morgan logo.

  <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/app-header/app-header-logo-treatment.png"
    alt="Example showing the logo layout construction."
    border
  />

Consider the following when placing your logo in the app header:

- Keep the aspect ratio of your logo when resizing it in each density. Consider visual balance and affordance. 
- You don't need to resize your logo to fit the max-height (size-base) of the branding area. 
- If preceded by the app name, the text should follow density aware body-text.
- Consider creating a compact version of your logo for small viewport experiences.

<Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/app-header/app-header-compact-logo.png"
    alt="Example showing the compact logo layout construction."
    border
  />

<GuidanceCallout type="positive" customPillText="Best practices">
- Always place the logo on the top-left corner of the application.
- You can place a title or app name in text form next to the logo.
- Link the logo to the app home page. 
- The logo should give users a sense of place while providing a large enough clickable target area.
</GuidanceCallout>

## Header only

In this layout, the app header is globally persistent. You can use it as standalone navigation for a small number of sections that don’t require secondary navigation. Although this layout provides more horizontal space for content, it has limited space for navigation items, and you may need to use combined navigation for complex hierarchies.

  <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/app-header/app-header-only.png"
    alt="Example of the header-only variant."
    border
  />

## Header with vertical navigation

The app header with vertical navigation offers an additional layer of hierarchy. This layout allows users to navigate complex structures and perform system and product tasks in the UI. Under this configuration, submenus can remain on display without interfering with the content. For more details about navigation hierarchy, visit the [navigation pattern](./navigation).  

  <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/app-header/app-header-vertical-navigation.png"
    alt="Header paired with vertical navigation."
    caption="An app header paired with vertical navigation."
    border
  />

## Responsive behavior

The app header is responsive to the width of the application viewport and responds dynamically to the [Salt breakpoints](/salt/foundations/responsiveness#breakpoints). As the app header scales down to fit smaller viewports, its elements adjust dynamically to provide the best possible user experience. 

For small viewport experiences, the app logo remains visible, while navigation and utility actions collapse into a hamburger menu positioned to the left of the brand logo. The navigation items will sit on top of the utility actions in the hierarchy of the vertical navigation. 

### Desktop

  <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/app-header/app-header-responsive-behavior-desktop.png"
    alt="App header with desktop layout for medium, large and extra large viewport experiences."
    caption="App header with desktop layout for medium, large and extra large viewport experiences."
    border
  />

### Mobile

  <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/app-header/app-header-responsive-behavior-mobile.png"
    alt="App header with mobile layout for extra small and small viewport experiences."
    caption="App header with mobile layout for extra small and small viewport experiences."
    border
  />

<GuidanceCallout type="positive" customPillText="Best practices">
 - Navigation items sit on top of the utility actions in the hierarchy of the hamburger menu.
 - If a search utility action is part of the app header, keep search functionality persistently available for small viewports. 
 - Consider medium, large and extra large [Salt breakpoints](/salt/foundations/responsiveness#breakpoints) for desktop experiences. 
 - Consider extra small and small [Salt breakpoints](/salt/foundations/responsiveness#breakpoints) for mobile experiences.
</GuidanceCallout>

## Sticky header position

The app header should sit in the north region, above the main, in a sticky position while the user scrolls down the page. This increases the discoverability of the elements in the header, where users can quickly access the navigation and utility actions elements without scrolling up to the top of the page. 

  <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/app-header/app-header-sticky-position.png"
    alt="The header stays in place while the user scrolls."
    caption="The header stays in place while the user scrolls."
    border
  />

## Bypass app header

If you're implementing a complex app header with several navigation items and utility actions, you should precede those header components with a skip link. This enables keyboard and screen reader users to shift focus quickly to the main page content and navigate your application more efficiently.

  <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/app-header/app-header-bypass-behavior.png"
    alt="Example of the 'Skip to content' link in the app header."
    caption="Example of the 'Skip to content' link in the app header."
    border
  />

:fragment{src="./fragments/feedback.mdx"}

# breadcrumbs.mdx

Source: https://github.com/jpmorganchase/salt-ds/blob/main/site/docs/patterns/breadcrumbs.mdx

title: Breadcrumbs
description: "Breadcrumbs are a secondary navigation pattern that helps users keep track of their current location within a hierarchy. It provides a space-efficient means of allowing quick navigation to previous levels."
layout: DetailPattern
tags:
  - pattern
aliases:
  - /salt/patterns/breadcrumbs
  resources:
    [
      { href: "https://storybook.saltdesignsystem.com/?path=/story/patterns-breadcrumbs--breadcrumbs", label: "Breadcrumbs examples" },
    ]
  components: ["Button", "Icon", "Link", "Text"]

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/breadcrumbs/breadcrumbs-hero-shot.png"
  alt="Example showing breadcrumbs."
  border
/>

## When to use

Use the pattern when the user navigates through related pages, or drills down into tables or charts. It provides further navigation relative to a users workflow/selection within their current area, page or widget. They are especially useful for identifying a location in a hierarchy when the user lands on a page via deep-linking from search or an external source. 

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/breadcrumbs/breadcrumbs-when.png"
  alt="Low-fi header paired with Breadcrumbs."
  border
/>

<GuidanceCallout type="positive" customPillText="Best practices">
- We recommend keeping the number of breadcrumb levels concise to a maximum of four, including the first level if it's displayed. Content is more easily discoverable when navigating a relatively wide and flat information hierarchy within applications. This prevents users from feeling overwhelmed.
- Use breadcrumbs to complement the application's main navigation—never to replace it.
- Don't show breadcrumbs when there is only one level in a hierarchy.
</GuidanceCallout>

## How to build

### Anatomy

Breadcrumbs contain:

1. **Breadcrumb:** Previous levels displayed as links icons separating them.
2. **Current level:** A text label showing the user’s current location.
3. **Overflow menu:** Use an overflow menu to show collapsed breadcrumbs.  

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/breadcrumbs/breadcrumbs-anatomy.png"
  alt="Breadcrumbs anatomy"
  border
/>

### Layout

- Use the [`Link`](/salt/components/link) component as the breadcrumb.
- Use the chevron-right [`Icon`](/salt/components/icon) as the separators.
- Use the icon only menu button for the overflow menu trigger. 

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/breadcrumbs/breadcrumbs-layout-1.png"
  alt="layout"
  border
/>

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/breadcrumbs/breadcrumbs-layout-2.png"
  alt="layout"
  border
/>

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/breadcrumbs/breadcrumbs-layout-3.png"
  alt="layout"
  border
/>

## Collapsed breadcrumbs

Breadcrumbs can be collapsed to save space or hide lower priority levels (e.g. only displaying Home and the current level). The hidden levels can be revealed in 2 different ways:

### Overflow menu

Use an overflow menu when there is not enough horizontal space available, the order of the menu items should match the hierarchy of the levels.

<ImageSwitcher
  images={[
    {
      src: "/img/patterns/breadcrumbs/breadcrumbs-collapsed-overflow-menu.png",
      alt: "Example showing collapsed breadcrumbs with an overflow menu.",
    },
    {
      src: "/img/patterns/breadcrumbs/breadcrumbs-collapsed-overflow-menu-expanded.png",
      alt: "Example showing collapsed breadcrumbs with an overflow menu active.",
    },
  ]}
  label="Show overflow menu"
/>

### Expansion

Alternatively (if there is sufficient horizontal space), use an use an expansion button to reveal all levels. Showing the levels inline can make the hierarchy of the levels more visible. 

<ImageSwitcher
  images={[
    {
      src: "/img/patterns/breadcrumbs/breadcrumbs-collapsed-expansion.png",
      alt: "Example showing collapsed breadcrumbs with expansion behavior.",
    },
    {
      src: "/img/patterns/breadcrumbs/breadcrumbs-collapsed-expansion-expanded.png",
      alt: "Example showing collapsed breadcrumbs with expansion behavior.",
    },
  ]}
  label="Show expansion"
/>

## Wrapped breadcrumbs

Wrap breadcrumbs when there is a need to keep the breadcrumb trail visible in the app, breadcrumbs can wrap onto subsequent lines. The breadcrumb and its separator should be on the same line.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/breadcrumbs/breadcrumbs-wrapped.png"
  alt="Example showing wrapped breadcrumbs"
  border
/>

## Shortened/contextual breadcrumbs

In some cases, you might want to hide breadcrumbs to make the path shorter or change breadcrumb labels to provide more context and help users understand the current task.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/breadcrumbs/breadcrumbs-shortened.png"
  alt="Example of shortened breadcrumbs. The levels “Settings” and “General” have been combined into one labelled “General Settings”."
  border
/>

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/breadcrumbs/breadcrumbs-contextual.png"
  alt="Example of contextual breadcrumb labels. “Profile” has been changed to “Edit Profile”."
  border
/>

# button-bar.mdx

Source: https://github.com/jpmorganchase/salt-ds/blob/main/site/docs/patterns/button-bar.mdx

title: Button bar
description: "A button bar displays possible actions for users to take when they reach the end of a task. You can use it to provide consistent presentation of button types and orders within pages or dialogs across your applications."
layout: DetailPattern
tags:
  - pattern
aliases:
  - /salt/patterns/button-bar
  resources:
    [
      { href: "https://storybook.saltdesignsystem.com/?path=/story/patterns-button-bar--button-bar", label: "Button bar examples" },
    ]
  components: ["Button", "Split layout", "Stack layout"]
  relatedPatterns: ["Forms"]

  <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/button-bar/button-bar-hero-shot.png"
    alt="Example button bar, with CTA to the left then primary. On the right side there are two secondary buttons."
    border
  />

## When to use

Use the pattern when the user needs to perform actions after reaching the end of a task in a page or a dialog. Some examples include:

- Navigating to previous or next steps
- Submitting a form
- Acknowledging or canceling changes

## How to build

### Anatomy

A button bar typically contains:

1. **Buttons**: possible actions for users to take.
2. **Groups**: used to visually communicate which buttons are related to each other.

  <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/button-bar/button-bar-anatomy.png"
    alt="A button bar anatomy."
    contentPosition="top"
    border
  />

### Layout

* Use [`Button`](/salt/components/button) to display actions in a button bar.
* Use [`StackLayout`](/salt/components/layouts/stack-layout) to group your buttons together.
* Use [`SplitLayout`](/salt/components/layouts/split-layout) to separate the button groups.

  <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/button-bar/button-bar-layout-1.png"
    alt="A button bar layout."
    contentPosition="top"
    border
  />

  <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/button-bar/button-bar-layout-2.png"
    alt="A button bar layout."
    contentPosition="top"
    border
  />

## Button options

There are three button appearances to choose from. Choosing the correct button depends on the context and is ultimately the choice of the application team. For guidance on button choices, please see the Button docs. We recommend using the accented button set for a majority of use cases, alongside the following guidelines for consistent design:

**Solid**
- Use for the primary path you intend the user to take.
- In almost all cases, your scenario should have one solid button within the button bar so the desired path is clear.
- This is commonly an affirmative action allowing users to proceed or complete the task, such as **Next**, **Save** or **Submit**.

**Bordered**
- Use for the secondary functions you're offering the user.
- There can be multiple equally weighted secondary functions within a button bar.
- You can use it as a dismissive action alongside the affirmative (solid) action, such as **Cancel** or **Dismiss**.

**Transparent**
- Use for the tertiary functions you're offering the user.
- There can be multiple equally weighted tertiary functions within a button bar.
- This is commonly a related task or function that’s lower priority than the secondary functions, such as **Import** or **Export**.

Remember to use a hierarchy when making your button choices, much like following a type ramp. In Example 1 below, Cancel is the alternate function and uses a solid button because there are only two options. However, in Example 2, Cancel uses the transparent button because three actions are available to the user, with this one being tertiary and the least desired option.

### Example 1

    - The **Submit** solid action uses the solid button.
    - The **Cancel** secondary action uses the bordered button.

  <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/button-bar/button-options-example-1.png"
    alt="Example showing button bar with Submit on the left as a solid, and Cancel as bordered to the right of Submit."
  />

### Example 2

    - The **Next** primary action uses the solid button.
    - The **Previous** alternate action uses the bordered button (order follows sequential forms).
    - The **Cancel** tertiary action uses the transparent button.

  <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/button-bar/button-options-example-2.png"
    alt="Example showing button bar with Next button on right as solid, Previous as bordered to the left of Next, and Cancel as transparent to the left of Previous."
  />

<GuidanceCallout type="positive" customPillText="Best practices">
  Provide only one solid button for a given task—the action that allows the user to complete the task.
</GuidanceCallout>

## Combining button sentiments

Optionally, use colored [sentiment buttons](/salt/components/button/examples#other-sentiments) within a button bar depending on the sentiment of the action - i.e. positive, caution and negative. We recommend combining a sentiment with the button appearance (solid, bordered or transparent) that best represents the importance of the action.

In the example below, the ‘Delete now’ button is styled using a solid appearance and negative sentiment to emphasize the risk of permanently deleting items as an action.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/button-bar/negative-sentiment-button.png"
  alt="Example showing a solid button with negative sentiment to emphasize the risk of permanently deleting items as an action."
  border
/>

## Button order

The container and the type of scenario determine the position of actions (solid, bordered and transparent buttons).

### Default/Single step form
    - Groups core actions on the left.
    - Follows an F-pattern reading model, allowing users to scan down quickly.

  <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/button-bar/vert-nav-layout-2.png"
    alt="Example showing default button bar order, Submit solid on the left and Cancel bordered to the right of Submit."
    border
  />
    
### Multi-step form
    - Groups core actions on the right.
    - Always positions **Next** right of **Previous** and **Cancel** to reflect the direction of the steps.

  <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/button-bar/vert-nav-layout-3.png"
    alt="Example showing form with button bar underneath and core actions on the right."
    border
  />

### Dialog
    - Always displays core actions on the right.
    - Follows a Z-pattern reading model, where actions are the last focal point in the dialog.

  <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/button-bar/vert-nav-layout-4.png"
    alt="Example showing a dialog with a form and button bar underneath. The core actions are on the right."
    border
  />

<GuidanceCallout type="positive" customPillText="Best practices">
  - Group core onward actions for the form to ensure they remain accessible on browser zoom (e.g., **Previous**, **Next**, **Cancel** or **Submit**).
  - You should display tertiary actions that aren’t core to the workflow at the opposite end of the button bar.
</GuidanceCallout>

## Button bar position

There are two ways to position the button bar.

### Fixed

Fix the button bar at the bottom of the viewport when:
- A user can proceed (or step back) regardless of task completion.
- The task is in a wizard.

If content overflows, the button bar uses a secondary border style.
<Diagrams>
  <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/button-bar/button-bar-fixed-1.png"
    alt="Example showing a form overflowing behind a button bar. The button bar has a top border."
    contentPosition="top"
    border
  >
  When fields overflow behind the button bar, a border should indicate if more fields are available. 
  </Diagram>
  <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/button-bar/button-bar-fixed-2.png"
    alt="Example showing the end of a form. The button bar has no top border."
    contentPosition="top"
    border
  >
  Hide the button bar border if content is no longer overflowing (i.e., the user has reached the bottom of the form or the form is entirely above the fold).
  </Diagram>
</Diagrams>

### In line

The button bar is located at the end of the task when:
- The user needs to complete the entire task before proceeding, for example, if there are mandatory fields in a form.
- The system needs the user to acknowledge all information on the page.

<Diagrams>
  <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/button-bar/button-bar-in-line-1.png"
    alt="Example showing an overflowing form."
    contentPosition="top"
    border
  >
  When the button bar is at the end of the task, the button may not be visible when the user is at the top.
  </Diagram>
  <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/button-bar/button-bar-in-line-2.png"
    alt="Example showing the bottom of a form with buttons."
    contentPosition="top"
    border
  >
  The button bar is visible when the user scrolls to the bottom of the task.
  </Diagram>
</Diagrams>

## Stacked button bar

For improved usability at smaller screen or app resolutions, we recommend responsively stacking the button bar when it reaches a specific viewport width or application breakpoint.

We recommend stacking at the xs breakpoint by default. Buttons will expand to fill the full width of the button bar when stacked.

Order of stacked buttons: In a stacked button layout, we recommend buttons stack in order of importance from the top down.

  <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/button-bar/vert-nav-layout-5.png"
    alt="Example button bar, vertically stacked."
    contentPosition="top"
    border
  />

<GuidanceCallout type="positive" customPillText="Best practices">
  - Enable the stacked layout when you have longer button labels that may not fit within the horizontal layout at smaller button bar widths.
  - If users will access your application on a mobile device, use a stacked button layout to ensure an adequate touch-area for the buttons.
</GuidanceCallout>

### Building a stacked button bar

1. Build a button bar following the foundational guidelines provided earlier in the documentation.
2. Adjust the direction property on both stack layout and split layout (if used) to `{{xs: "column", sm: "row"}}`. This responsive setting arranges the buttons into a column for extra small (xs) screens and a row for small (sm) screens and upwards. This ensures a responsive layout that adapts to the viewport width.
3. When the button bar has core actions on the right, you'll need to configure an alternative stack layout.
    - Reverse the buttons in this layout to ensure that the core actions are at the top.
    - Employ Salt's responsive design utilities to render this alternative layout at the desired breakpoint. You can refer to our [examples](https://storybook.saltdesignsystem.com/?path=/story/patterns-button-bar--responsive-reverse) for more information.

  <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/button-bar/button-bar-building-stacked-button-bar-1.png"
    alt="Diagram showing how to build a stacked button bar."
    contentPosition="top"
    border
  />

  <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/button-bar/button-bar-building-stacked-button-bar-2.png"
    alt="Diagram showing how to build a stacked button bar."
    contentPosition="top"
    border
  />

:fragment{src="./fragments/feedback.mdx"}

# comments.mdx

Source: https://github.com/jpmorganchase/salt-ds/blob/main/site/docs/patterns/comments.mdx

title: Comments
description: "The Comments pattern enables users to post, view, and interact with user-generated content, such as feedback, discussions, or reviews."
layout: DetailPattern
tags:
  - pattern
aliases:
  - /salt/patterns/comments
  resources:
    [
      { href: "https://storybook.saltdesignsystem.com/?path=/story/patterns-comments", label: "Comments examples" },
    ]
  components: ["Avatar", "Form field", "Input", "Multiline input"]

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/comments/comments-hero-shot.png"
  srcDark="/img/patterns/comments/comments-hero-shot-dark.png"
  alt="Example showing comments."
  border
/>

## When to use

- Facilitate team communication, feedback, or discussion within an application.
- Capture collaborative notes and reminders in shared contexts.
- Maintain an auditable discussion log.
- Suitable for forums, activity feeds, support threads, and collaborative workspaces.

## How to build

### Anatomy

At the top level, Comments consists of an input for adding new comments and a running list that shows the conversation history, so users can review prior messages.

Each comment tile can include:

1. **Author**: Display name 
2. **Avatar (optional)**: Initials or image identifying the commenter.
3. **Supporting details**: Metadata such as timestamp, an optional user role, or an “Edited” indicator.
4. **Content**: Main body of the comment.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/comments/comments-anatomy.png"
  srcDark="/img/patterns/comments/comments-anatomy-dark.png"
  alt="Comments anatomy"
  border
/>

### Layout

Use [`StackLayout`](/salt/components/layouts/stack-layout) to display the input and the comments list. 

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/comments/comments-layout.png"
  srcDark="/img/patterns/comments/comments-layout-dark.png"
  alt="comments layout"
  border
/>

## Avatar and user role 

Include when identity cues improve scanning or clarify ownership.

- Avatar: Show a photo; fall back to initials. Keep size and placement consistent.
- Role: Use a short, standardized role or title. 

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/comments/comments-avatar.png"
  srcDark="/img/patterns/comments/comments-avatar-dark.png"
  alt="comments with avatars"
  border
/>

Use the [`Avatar`](/salt/components/avatar) component’s categorical colors to differentiate authors.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/comments/comments-user-role.png"
  srcDark="/img/patterns/comments/comments-user-role-dark.png"
  alt="comments with user roles"
  border
/>

## Timestamp

Always show a timestamp and the last edit time.
<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/comments/comments-timestamp.png"
  srcDark="/img/patterns/comments/comments-timestamp-dark.png"
  alt="comments with time stamp"
  border
/>

<GuidanceCallout type="positive" customPillText="Best practices">
  - Display “edited” with the last edit time; keep the original creation timestamp visible.
  - Use locale‑aware formatting and the viewer’s time zone.
</GuidanceCallout>

## Empty state

Use a short, neutral message to indicate there are no comments yet.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/comments/comments-empty-state.png"
  srcDark="/img/patterns/comments/comments-empty-state-dark.png"
  alt="Comments with empty state"
  border
/>

<GuidanceCallout type="positive" customPillText="Best practices">
  - Use direct language that sets expectations (for example, “No comments yet.”).
  - Keep it compact; avoid decorative imagery or filler.
</GuidanceCallout>

## Multiline input

Use a [`MultilineInput`](/salt/components/multiline-input) when longer messages are common; this reduces scrolling while composing.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/comments/comments-multiline-input.png"
  srcDark="/img/patterns/comments/comments-multiline-input-dark.png"
  alt="Comments with multiline input"
  border
/>

<GuidanceCallout type="positive" customPillText="Best practices">
  - Use a multiline field only if a meaningful portion of users will benefit.
  - Auto‑grow to a sensible maximum height, then scroll within the field so the thread stays visible.
</GuidanceCallout>

## Display order

Choose the order that best fits the task.

- Newest-first (default for ongoing threads): Surfaces the latest activity immediately; ideal for long‑running discussions over days or weeks.
- Oldest-first: Preserves chronological reading; best for short, time‑boxed reviews where sequence matters.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/comments/comments-display-order.png"
  srcDark="/img/patterns/comments/comments-display-order-dark.png"
  alt="Comments display order"
  border
/>

## Submission error

Offer recovery without losing work by showing an inline error. Preserve the failed comment text.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/comments/comments-submission-error.png"
  srcDark="/img/patterns/comments/comments-submission-error-dark.png"
  alt="Comments with submission error"
  border
/>

<GuidanceCallout type="positive" customPillText="Best practices">
  - Use clear, actionable copy that states what happened and what the user can do next.
  - Provide Retry and Dismiss actions; keep the message visible until resolved.
  - Support stacked errors if multiple submissions fail.
</GuidanceCallout>

# contact-details.mdx

Source: https://github.com/jpmorganchase/salt-ds/blob/main/site/docs/patterns/contact-details.mdx

title: Contact details
description: "Contact details display communication information for a person, company, distribution list or individual channel. This can include a name, a phone number or email address."
layout: DetailPattern
tags:
  - pattern
aliases:
  - /salt/patterns/contact-details
  resources:
    [
      { href: "https://storybook.saltdesignsystem.com/?path=/story/patterns-contact-details--contact-details", label: "Examples" },
    ]
  components: ["Avatar", "Button", "Flow layout", "Icon", "Stack layout", "Text", "Tooltip"]

 <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/contact-details/contact-details.png"
    alt="Contact details how to build"
    border
  />

## When to use

Use this pattern to:
- Provide details and direct channels of communication for sales or support purposes.
- Display contact information in a directory or CRM (Customer Relationship Management) system.
- Allow users to populate form fields in a workflow with details from a list of contacts, e.g., client contact selection for a ticket.

<GuidanceCallout type="positive" customPillText="Best practices">
Consider a data grid when you need to display many contacts with a standardized set of contact information.
</GuidanceCallout>

## How to build

### Anatomy

The contact details pattern comprises an avatar and text elements:

1. **Avatar**: A visual representation of the contact that provides a point of reference at glance.
2. **Header**: Contains the name of the contact. Optionally, use text to display further information such as company names or company ID.
3. **Additional details**: Relevant meta data, e.g., role, location, phone number or email. You can define the details as links, making them interactive, to enable immediate communication to a contact from within your application.

<Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/contact-details/contact-details-anatomy.png"
    alt="Contact details with component annotations"
    border
/>

<GuidanceCallout type="positive" customPillText="Best practices">
Keep label lengths similar to ensure close proximity to their respective values. If you’re displaying supplementary details, we recommend that you left align their labels.
</GuidanceCallout>

### Layout

Use [`StackLayout`](/salt/components/layouts/stack-layout) to display the avatar and all text elements that make up contact details in a row.

 <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/contact-details/contact-details-layout-1.png"
    alt="Contact Details with layout annotations"
    border
  />

Use `StackLayout` to display the additional details in a row.

 <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/contact-details/contact-details-layout-2.png"
    alt="Contact Details with layout annotations"
    border
  />

Use `StackLayout` to display the header and additional details section in a column.

 <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/contact-details/contact-details-layout-3.png"
    alt="Contact Details with layout annotations"
    border
  />

## Using icons

You can use icon descriptors as a visually concise alternative to textual labels—to help users quickly identify the available communication channels.

 <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/contact-details/contact-details-icons.png"
    alt="Contact Details using Icon Descriptors"
    caption="An example of contact details using descriptive icons."
    border
  />

<GuidanceCallout type="positive" customPillText="Best practices">
Refrain from using icon descriptors when you have multiple values for similar channels, such as work and cellphone numbers.
</GuidanceCallout>

## Using links

We recommend emails to be interactive links by default, you can also define other details (e.g. phone number) as links, making them interactive—to enable immediate communication to a contact from within your application.

 <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/contact-details/contact-details-using-links.png"
    alt="Contact Details using links"
    caption="An example of contact details using links."
    border
  />

## In a container

You can embed contact details in a range of container components. 

This example demonstrates the component embedded within a [card](/salt/components/card).

 <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/contact-details/contact-details-card.png"
    alt="Contact Details Embedded in a Card"
    caption="Contact details embedded within a card."
    border
  />

## Quick actions

You can define quick actions, one-click shortcuts to specific functions or features. This can include starting a new email in Outlook, or calling a contact in Zoom.

Ensure that quick action buttons have a tooltip displayed as per the [icon only button best practices](https://www.saltdesignsystem.com/salt/components/button/examples#icon-only).

For layout guidance, refer to the [button bar pattern](/salt/patterns/button-bar).

 <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/contact-details/contact-details-actions.png"
    alt="Contact Details with quick actions button bar"
    caption="Contact details with a quick actions button bar."
    border
  />

## Collapsible

If you’re displaying supplementary details, you can configure them to be collapsible.

 <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/contact-details/contact-details-collapsible-spacing.png"
    alt="Contact Details with collapsible details"
    caption="Contact details with collapsible details."
    border
  />

   <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/contact-details/contact-details-collapsible-layout.png"
    alt="Collapsible detail layout"
    caption="Use a split layout between quick actions and the collapsible button."
    border
  />

<GuidanceCallout type="positive" customPillText="Best practices">
Consider making supplementary details collapsible when they contain secondary information, and don’t need to be always on display.
</GuidanceCallout>

## List version

The list version allows you to display a snapshot of key details. It’s ideal when you have restricted real estate, such as in a client picker dropdown menu or a contact directory list.

To show as many options as possible, we recommend you keep data points to no more than one line. Prioritize the most important values. 

The link function won't be able to be applied to the text content (e.g. email or phone number) as it is an list item that users select as a whole option from the dropdown.

 <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/contact-details/contact-details-list.png"
    alt="Contact Details in list"
    caption="Contact details in a list."
    border
  />

Use `StackLayout` to display the text elements underneath the header in a row.

 <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/contact-details/contact-details-list-layout-1.png"
    alt="Contact Details in list using stack layout."
    border
  />

 <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/contact-details/contact-details-list-layout-2.png"
    alt="Contact Details in list using stack layout."
    border
  />

# content-status.mdx

Source: https://github.com/jpmorganchase/salt-ds/blob/main/site/docs/patterns/content-status.mdx

title: Content status
description: "A content status provides information about content in a container component of an application. It remains onscreen until a situation resolves or the user takes action, making it a great tool for communication and guidance."
layout: DetailPattern
tags:
  - pattern
aliases:
  - /salt/patterns/content-status
  resources:
    [
      { href: "https://storybook.saltdesignsystem.com/?path=/story/patterns-content-status--info", label: "Examples" }
    ]
  components: ["Button", "Progress", "Spinner", "Stack layout", "Status indicator", "Text"]

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/content-status/content-status.png"
  alt="Example showing a content status with an info indicator"
  border
/>

## When to use

Use this pattern in a container component:
- When content is loading.
- To share information with users.
- To let users know there’s an error.
- When the user has successfully submitted content.

## How to build

### Anatomy

The content status consists of three functional areas:

1. **Visual indicator:** Content status can use [`StatusIndicator`](/salt/components/status-indicator), [`Progress`](/salt/components/progress) or [`Spinner`](/salt/components/spinner) for its visual indicator.
2. **Text:** Text elements serve as supporting messages.
3. **Button:** Buttons are optional and can be added to reload content or perform a custom action.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/content-status/content-status-anatomy.png"
  alt="Example showing a content status anatomy"
  border
  content="Content status functional areas."
/>

### Layout

- Use [`StackLayout`](/salt/components/layouts/stack-layout) to display the two lists and move buttons that make up list builder in a row formation.
- Use [`Text`](/salt/components/text), [`Button`](/salt/components/button) and [`Input`](/salt/components/input) to assemble the header area.
- Use [`StackLayout`](/salt/components/layouts/stack-layout) to orient the move buttons between the two lists in a column formation.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/content-status/content-status-layout.png"
  alt="Example showing a content status with components and spacing labeled"
  border
  content="Anatomy of content status."
/>

<GuidanceCallout type="positive" customPillText="Best practices">
- Text line length shouldn't exceed 80 characters. See the [typography foundation](/salt/foundations/typography) for more information.
- You should horizontally and vertically center the pattern in the container.
</GuidanceCallout>

### Supporting messages

- **Have a clear hierarchy**: Your titles should be stand-alone, revealing key information your users need to know without relying on the supporting message, which users may skim over, e.g., “Login required.”
- **Be helpful**: If it’s possible for your users to resolve or rectify an issue, make sure you state this clearly, e.g., “You can log in to access this data.”
- **Keep it simple**: Try to limit titles to a single line and supporting messages to no more than three lines.

## Loading content

We've used a [progress](/salt/components/progress) component in this example to help manage user expectations. If you know how much of a current process is complete, use this to communicate that information.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/content-status/content-status-loading.png"
  alt="Example showing a content status with a progress indicator"
  caption="Example showing a content status with a progress indicator."
  border
/>

We've used a [spinner](/salt/components/spinner) component to reassure users in this example. Use this to let your users know that content is loading or processing without sharing an exact time frame.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/content-status/content-status-loading-small.png"
  alt="Example showing a content status with a spinner"
  caption="Example showing a content status with a spinner."
  border
/>

## Info message

Use this variant to communicate useful information. For example, if there’s no data available, this variation can communicate that message to let users know why they can't see any content.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/content-status/content-status-info.png"
  alt="Example showing a content status with an info indicator"
  caption="Example showing a content status with an info indicator."
  border
/>

## Warning message

Use the warning status to inform users of an issue or potential issue related to their current task. Use this for issues that don't prevent the user from continuing or completing their task. This could include a system status that may cause issues at a later point.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/content-status/content-status-warning.png"
  alt="Example showing a content status with a warning indicator"
  caption="Example showing a content status with a warning indicator."
  border
/>

## Error message

Use the error status to communicate a critical issue that prevents the user from continuing or completing the task. This could include missing content or user information required.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/content-status/content-status-error.png"
  alt="Example showing a content status with an error indicator"
  caption="Example showing a content status with an error indicator."
  border
/>

<GuidanceCallout type="positive" customPillText="Best practices">
 Error and warning messages should: 
 1. Notify users when there’s an issue. 
 2. Identify and explain the issue. 
 3. Provide a resolution.
</GuidanceCallout>

## Success message

This example lets users know that content has been successfully processed, e.g., the user has completed and submitted a form.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/content-status/content-status-success.png"
  alt="Example showing a content status with a success indicator"
  caption="Example showing a content status with a success indicator."
  border
/>

## Label only

Use the label only content status when you:

- Have limited space.
- Don’t want to display spinners due to performance concerns, e.g., on low performance devices.
- Want to avoid busy visual UI and animations.

For example, use for displaying a loading status in a data grid or in a combo box list.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/content-status/content-status-label-only.png"
  alt="Example showing a content status with a success indicator"
  border
  caption="Example showing a content status with a label only."
/>
