# keyboard-shortcuts.mdx

Source: https://github.com/jpmorganchase/salt-ds/blob/main/site/docs/patterns/keyboard-shortcuts.mdx

title: Keyboard shortcuts
description: "Keyboard shortcuts allow users to execute actions, that are usually performed with a mouse or trackpad, using a keyboard. They increase the efficiency and productivity of users who primarily rely on their keyboard when interacting with applications."
layout: DetailPattern
tags:
  - pattern
aliases:
  - /salt/patterns/keyboard-shortcuts
  resources:
    [
      { href: "https://storybook.saltdesignsystem.com/?path=/story/patterns-keyboard-shortcuts--with-dialog", label: "Examples" },
    ]
  components: ["Input", "Kbd", "Switch", "Table"]
The keyboard shortcuts pattern is a comprehensive and searchable list of the shortcuts that are currently available to the application user, helping them to quickly reference and learn key combinations and perform actions efficiently.

This pattern is a recommended layout and should be displayed within an appropriate container component that fits the application's information architecture and supports the user's workflow.

 <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/keyboard-shortcuts/keyboard-shortcuts-pattern-example.png"
    srcDark="/img/patterns/keyboard-shortcuts/keyboard-shortcuts-pattern-example-dark.png"
    alt="Keyboard Shortcuts pattern example, showing the actions and respective key combinations side by side"
    border
    background="secondary"
  />

## How to build

### Anatomy

1. **Keyboard shortcuts switch**: Allows users to enable or disable application keyboard shortcuts.
2. **Filter**: Allows users to quickly search and discover specific shortcuts by typing keywords.
3. **Action name**: User-initiated commands—such as Save or Delete—that correspond to defined shortcuts. 
4. **Description**: A brief description for actions that are unique to your application or require additional context to help users understand their purpose.
3. **Key**: Keyboard shortcuts use a combination of modifier keys and character keys to perform actions.

 <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/keyboard-shortcuts/keyboard-shortcuts-pattern-anatomy.png"
    srcDark="/img/patterns/keyboard-shortcuts/keyboard-shortcuts-pattern-anatomy-dark.png"
    alt="The anatomy of the Keyboard Shortcuts Pattern, with numbers indicating the position of the examples given"
    border
    background="secondary"
  />

<Callout status="success" title="Best practices" >
  Use concise and descriptive names for actions to reflect the UI command executed by the shortcut.
</Callout>

### Layout

- Use [Switch](/salt/components/switch) to display keyboard shortcuts on/off switch.
- Use [Combo box](/salt/components/combo-box) to display search field.
- Use [Table](/salt/components/table) to display keyboard shortcut list.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/keyboard-shortcuts/keyboard-shortcuts-pattern-layout.png"
  srcDark="/img/patterns/keyboard-shortcuts/keyboard-shortcuts-pattern-layout-dark.png"
  alt="The layout of the Keyboard Shortcuts pattern, showing how other components are used within it"
  border
  background="secondary"
/>

## When to use

Use this pattern to:
- Display a comprehensive and searchable list of keyboard shortcuts available in the application.
- Help users quickly reference, discover, and learn key combinations, improving efficiency, accessibility, and overall user experience.

<Callout status="success" title="Best practices" >
  Provide keyboard shortcuts as an alternative to mouse or trackpad interactions, supporting users who prefer or require keyboard input.
</Callout>

## How it works

### Searching shortcuts

1. The keyboard shortcuts initially displays all available shortcuts.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/keyboard-shortcuts/keyboard-shortcuts-pattern-searching-shortcuts-default.png"
  srcDark="/img/patterns/keyboard-shortcuts/keyboard-shortcuts-pattern-searching-shortcuts-default-dark.png"
  alt="The Keyboard Shortcuts Pattern in its initial state, showing all shortcuts"
  border
  background="secondary"
/>

2. When the user enters text in the filter input, the list updates to show only the matching shortcuts. For guidance on filtering behavior, refer to the [List Filtering pattern](/salt/patterns/list-filtering) page.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/keyboard-shortcuts/keyboard-shortcuts-pattern-searching-shortcuts-results.png"
  srcDark="/img/patterns/keyboard-shortcuts/keyboard-shortcuts-pattern-searching-shortcuts-results-dark.png"
  alt="The Keyboard Shortcuts Pattern showing search results after inputting a word"
  border
  background="secondary"
/>

### Enabling or Disabling Keyboard Shortcuts

Allow users to control keyboard shortcuts with a switch. When shortcuts are disabled, the shortcut list should be hidden.

<Callout status="success" title="Best practices" >
  Provide users with the option to disable keyboard shortcuts to enhance usability and accessibility. This is especially important in applications with custom shortcuts, as it helps prevent accidental activation and reduces user frustration.
</Callout>

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/keyboard-shortcuts/keyboard-shortcuts-pattern-enabling-disabling-shortcuts.png"
  srcDark="/img/patterns/keyboard-shortcuts/keyboard-shortcuts-pattern-enabling-disabling-shortcuts-dark.png"
  alt="a block diagram showing how to enable and disable the Keyboard Shortcuts pattern"
  border
  background="secondary"
/>

### Scrolling keyboard shortcuts

If the keyboard shortcuts list exceeds the available display area, an overflow shadow and scrollbar should be displayed to help the user navigate the list and recognize that more shortcuts are available.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/keyboard-shortcuts/keyboard-shortcuts-pattern-scrolling-shortcuts.png"
  srcDark="/img/patterns/keyboard-shortcuts/keyboard-shortcuts-pattern-scrolling-shortcuts-dark.png"
  alt="The keyboard Shortcuts pattern showing a vertical scrollbar with overflowing content"
  border
  background="secondary"
/>

### Choosing a container for the keyboard shortcuts

This pattern should be placed inside the appropriate container for your application. Select a container that aligns with the product’s user experience and context of use. Common options include:

- [Dialog](salt/components/dialog): Suitable when users need to focus on shortcuts without distraction, and when shortcuts should be accessible from anywhere in the application through a keyboard shortcut—quickly and without disrupting common tasks.
-  [Preferences dialog](salt/patterns/preferences-dialog): Works well if keyboard shortcuts are part of broader settings.
- [Drawer](salt/components/drawer): Appropriate for persistent access, or when shortcut settings are relevant to a specific part of the application that is in focus.

The choice of container should be guided by how and when users will need to access the shortcuts, ensuring the pattern effectively supports the intended task.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/keyboard-shortcuts/keyboard-shortcuts-in-dialog.png"
  srcDark="/img/patterns/keyboard-shortcuts/keyboard-shortcuts-in-dialog-dark.png"
  alt="the Keyboard Shortcuts pattern located inside a dialog"
  border
  background="secondary"
/>

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/keyboard-shortcuts/keyboard-shortcuts-in-preferences-dialog.png"
  srcDark="/img/patterns/keyboard-shortcuts/keyboard-shortcuts-in-preferences-dialog-dark.png"
  alt="The Keyboard Shortcuts pattern located inside a preferences dialog"
  border
  background="secondary"
/>

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/keyboard-shortcuts/keyboard-shortcuts-in-drawer.png"
  srcDark="/img/patterns/keyboard-shortcuts/keyboard-shortcuts-in-drawer-dark.png"
  alt="The Keyboard Shortcuts pattern located inside a drawer"
  border
  background="secondary"
/>

## How to define shortcuts

When defining your shortcuts, we recommend taking the following steps:

- Consider whether each shortcut should be global or contextual.
- Combine one modifier key with a character key that's associated with the name of the action (e.g., "Cmd + S" for Save).
- Use a maximum of three keys, at least one of which must be a modifier key.
- Test your shortcuts on multiple keyboard layouts, operating systems, platforms, and browsers to ensure they are easy to use and do not conflict with essential system or browser shortcuts.
- Avoid ambiguous or hard-to-reach keys—prefer letters and numbers over symbols, as some characters (like the £ sign) are not universally available or may require complex key combinations on certain layouts.
- Clearly document shortcuts for each operating system.

<Callout status="success" title="Best practices" >
  If your application includes shortcuts bound to a single character, you must comply with the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.1. For further information, please refer to the Accessibility section below.
</Callout>

### Global vs Contextual shortcuts

When setting up keyboard shortcuts for your application, consider both global and contextual shortcuts. 

<Table>
  <THead>
    <tr>
      <th></th>
      <th>Global shortcuts</th>
      <th>Contextual shortcuts</th>
    </tr>
  </THead>
  <TBody>
    <tr>
      <td>Definition</td>
      <td>Available throughout the application, regardless of focus</td>
      <td>Active only when specific elements are focused</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
     <td>Example use case</td>
      <td>Saving a document from any screen</td>
      <td>Selecting text in an input field</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Example shortcut</td>
      <td><Kbd>Ctrl/Cmd</Kbd> + <Kbd>S</Kbd></td>
     <td><Kbd>Ctrl/Cmd</Kbd> + <Kbd>A</Kbd></td>
    </tr>
  </TBody>
</Table>

### Modifier and Character keys

#### Modifier keys

When the user presses a modifier key at the same time as another key, the default function of that key is modified—and together they execute the assigned shortcut. Cmd, Ctrl, Shift and Alt are examples of keys that you can use to modify other keys. Modifier keys can differ depending on the platform.

<Table>
  <THead>
    <tr>
      <th colSpan="1">Platform</th>
      <th colSpan="4">Modifiers</th>
    </tr>
  </THead>
  <TBody>
    <tr>
      <td>macOS</td>
      <td>Ctrl</td>
      <td>Shift</td>
      <td>Option</td>
      <td>Cmd</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
     <td>Windows</td>
      <td>Ctrl</td>
      <td>Shift</td>
      <td>Alt</td>
      <td>Win</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Linux</td>
      <td>Ctrl</td>
      <td>Shift</td>
      <td>Alt</td>
      <td>Meta</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Bloomberg</td>
      <td>Ctrl</td>
      <td>Shift</td>
      <td>Alt</td>
      <td>Go</td>
    </tr>
  </TBody>
</Table>

<Callout title="Bloomberg Keyboards">

Bloomberg keyboards, common in financial environments, feature a distinctive orange "Go" key used to execute commands. When designing shortcuts for these keyboards, consider supporting the "Go" key and avoid conflicts with Bloomberg’s built-in shortcuts. Always test your shortcuts for compatibility.

</Callout>

#### Character keys

It is recommended to display up to three character keys in a keyboard shortcut. Make sure at least one of the keys has a close association to the action that the shortcut executes—for example, "Cmd + S" for the Save action. This will make it easier for users to memorize keyboard shortcuts they'll use frequently.

Common character keys include:

<Table>
  <THead>
    <tr>
      <th>Key Type</th>
      <th>Modifier keys</th>
    </tr>
  </THead>
  <TBody>
    <tr>
      <td>Letters</td>
      <td>a-z</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
     <td>Numbers</td>
      <td>0-9</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Function Keys</td>
      <td>F1-F19</td>
    </tr>
     <tr>
      <td>Punctuation</td>
      <td>', -, =, [, ], , ;, *, ,, ., /</td>
    </tr>
     <tr>
      <td>Navigation</td>
      <td>Left, Up, Right, Down, PageUp, PageDown, End, Home</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Other</td>
      <td>Tab, Enter, Escape, Space, Backspace, Delete, Pause/Break, CapsLock, Insert</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Numpad</td>
      <td>Numpad0–Numpad9, Numpad_multiply, Numpad_add, Numpad_separator, Numpad_subtract, Numpad_decimal, Numpad_divide</td>
    </tr>
  </TBody>
</Table>

<Callout status="success" title="Best practices" >
  When designing keyboard shortcuts, always ensure your chosen combination does not conflict with important pre-existing shortcuts or reserved browser hotkeys. To manage potential conflicts:
  - Use a different modifier key (e.g., Ctrl, Alt, Shift).
  - Consider the second character key in the action’s name.
  - Add an extra character key if needed, but keep the total to no more than three keys for usability.

  Some hotkeys cannot be overridden, as they are reserved by browsers to maintain user safety and a consistent browsing experience. Always verify that your shortcut does not interfere with these reserved combinations.
</Callout>

## Technical note

### Integrating third party keyboard shortcut libraries

In our examples, we use the react-hotkeys-hook library to demonstrate keyboard shortcut implementation. It offers a simple and intuitive API for handling keyboard events, enabling you to add shortcut functionality with minimal setup. For installation instructions and detailed API usage, please refer to the official library [documentation](https://react-hotkeys-hook.vercel.app/).

## Accessibility

Providing keyboard functionality is essential for accessibility. 

Users with visual or mobility impairments may rely entirely on the keyboard, and many power users prefer keyboard shortcuts for efficiency. By implementing the keyboard shortcuts pattern, you enhance the user experience for everyone.

It’s important to note that adding keyboard shortcuts alone does not guarantee full keyboard accessibility. All interactive elements in your application should remain accessible through standard keyboard navigation, such as using Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, and Space keys to move focus and activate controls.

### WCAG 2.1 keyboard requirements

If you have shortcuts that are bound to only a single character, you must meet a requirement in the 2.1 version of the [Web Content Accessibility Guidelines](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG21/Understanding/character-key-shortcuts.html). Make sure you provide a mechanism to toggle the shortcuts on/off, remap them to different keys or (if they're related to a particular element) make them active only when that element has focus.

# list-builder.mdx

Source: https://github.com/jpmorganchase/salt-ds/blob/main/site/docs/patterns/list-builder.mdx

title: List builder
description: "A list builder allows users to create a bespoke list of items from an original list, also known as a pick list, adding or removing items as required. Users can filter the items by using the filter input field."
layout: DetailPattern
tags:
  - pattern
aliases:
  - /salt/patterns/list-builder
  resources:
    [
      { href: "https://storybook.saltdesignsystem.com/?path=/story/patterns-list-builder--single-select", label: "List builder examples" },
    ]
  components: ["List", "Input", "Button", "Text", "Stack layout"]
  relatedPatterns: ["List filtering"]

  <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/list-builder/list-builder.png"
    alt="An example of a list builder."
    contentPosition="top"
    border
  />

## When to use

Use this pattern when users need to customize a list from a selection of options. 

List builders are useful when you want to distinguish selected items from a larger list of available items. This is particularly useful when the initial list is so large that it's difficult to see which items the user has selected. With the two lists side-by-side, users can easily view or compare selected and available options.

Typical use cases for using a list builder include:
- Choosing visible columns or chart series from a dataset.
- Customizing a client, account or research list in a CRM (customer relationship management system).
- Creating a distribution list.
- Creating a list of accounts for use in transactions.

<GuidanceCallout type="positive" customPillText="Best practices">
- Apply a consistent logic to the order of displayed items. Display pick list items chronologically or in alphabetical order, provided there are no pre-defined requirements.
- Only use a list builder when there are at least five items to choose from. If you have fewer items, use a single re-orderable list.
</GuidanceCallout>

## How to build

### Anatomy

The list builder has three functional areas:

1. **Header**: Contains a list label (with optional item count), a button bar and a [filter](/salt/patterns/list-filtering).
2. **List**: Serves as the container for the list items (multi-select or single-select).
3. **Move buttons**: Provides functionality to move items between the two lists.

  <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/list-builder/list-builder-anatomy.png"
    alt="Anatomy of a list builder"
    contentPosition="top"
    border
  />

<GuidanceCallout type="positive" customPillText="Best practices">
Apply a consistent logic to the order of displayed items. Display pick list items chronologically or in alphabetical order, provided there are no predefined requirements.
</GuidanceCallout>

### Layout

- Use [`StackLayout`](/salt/components/layouts/stack-layout) to display the two lists and move buttons that make up the list builder in a row formation.
- Use [`Text`](/salt/components/text), [`Button`](/salt/components/button) and [`Input`](/salt/components/input) to assemble the header area.
- Use `StackLayout` to orient the move buttons between the two lists in a column formation.

  <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/list-builder/list-builder-layout.png"
    alt="Layout for a list builder."
    contentPosition="top"
    border
  />

## Position of added items

There are two common behaviors for positioning selected items within the list:

1. **Automatic end positioning**: Moving an item from the pick list automatically places it at the end of the selected item list. In a large list where scrolling is necessary, always adjust the view to display the newly added item.
2. **Relative positioning**: If a user has an item selected in the added list, moving an item from the pick list to the selected item list positions it after the selected item. This maintains the relative order within the added list.

When moving items from the selected item list back to the pick list, position them according to the pick list's existing sort order. This makes items in large pick lists as quick and easy to find as possible.

<GuidanceCallout type="positive" customPillText="Best practices">
- Change list labels based on your use case. Make sure to keep them clear and concise.
- Always display a label for ADA compliance and to help users identify the purpose of the list, for example, a list of available/picked columns within a grid.
- Show a count in brackets to help users keep track of the number of items in the list.
- Incorporate more buttons into the button bar according to your use case. Examples include “move to top” and “move to bottom” functionalities.
</GuidanceCallout>

## Multiple selection

Users can move multiple items in a single action between the pick list and the selected item list using the list builder, allowing movement in both directions.

  <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/list-builder/multi-select-list-builder.png"
    alt="Multiple selections with a list builder."
    contentPosition="top"
    border
    caption="Multiple selections with a list builder."
  />

## Single selection

Single selection allows users to move only one item at a time between the pick list and the selected item list.

  <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/list-builder/single-select-list-builder.png"
    alt="Single selection with a list builder."
    contentPosition="top"
    border
    caption="Single selection with a list builder."
  />

## Non re-orderable

If users don’t need to reorder items in the new list, remove this feature.

  <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/list-builder/non-reorderable-list-builder.png"
    alt="Single selection with a list builder."
    contentPosition="top"
    border
    caption="In the above example, the header lacks reordering controls."
  />

## Empty state message

Display a message to prompt or instruct the user when a list is empty. You can customize this message. Make sure that the text is concise, descriptive and clearly understood. Use the [content status pattern](/salt/patterns/content-status) to display empty state messages.

  <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/list-builder/empty-list.png"
    alt="An empty state message."
    contentPosition="top"
    border
    caption="An empty state message."
  />

<GuidanceCallout type="positive" customPillText="Best practices">
Horizontally and vertically center the empty state message in the container.
</GuidanceCallout>

## Stack layout

Use a stack layout to compose the list builder vertically for interfaces with limited viewport width, such as mobile devices. 

  <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/list-builder/stack-layout-list-builder.png"
    alt="A vertically aligned list builder."
    contentPosition="top"
    border
    caption="A vertically aligned list builder using a stack layout."
  />

<GuidanceCallout type="positive" customPillText="Best practices">
Use a minimum width of 8ems and ensure that the list builder spans the full width of the screen or its parent container.
</GuidanceCallout>

## Filter and sort

In both the pick list and the selected item list, users can [apply filters](/salt/patterns/list-filtering) with the input field, enabling real-time filtration from a large data set. The list dynamically refreshes to display only the items that match the search criteria.

  <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/list-builder/filtering-list.png"
    alt="Filter and sort behaviors for a list builder."
    contentPosition="top"
    border
    caption="Filter and sort behaviors for a list builder."
  />

<GuidanceCallout type="positive" customPillText="Best practices">
Include a sort button within the pick list, enabling users to organize the list in either ascending or descending order.
</GuidanceCallout>

# list-filtering.mdx

Source: https://github.com/jpmorganchase/salt-ds/blob/main/site/docs/patterns/list-filtering.mdx

title: List filtering
description: "When searching through a list, a filter enables users to specify criteria and only show relevant options. This pattern introduces the filter behavior of Salt components where a list is used."
layout: DetailPattern
tags:
  - pattern
aliases:
  - /salt/patterns/list-filtering
  components: ["Input", "List", "Spinner"]
  relatedPatterns: ["List builder"]

  <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/list-filtering/list-filter.png"
    alt="A list filter."
    contentPosition="top"
    border
  />

## When to use

Use filtering when you have a lengthy list that users have to scroll to view all available options. The pattern typically comprises input and list based components to use a string to filter items for quick selection.

List filtering is a common behavior found in:
* [`ComboBox`](/salt/components/combo-box)
* [List builder](/salt/patterns/list-builder)
* Pivot table
* Tree builder

## Filter logic 

When filtering results, we recommend:

* Case-insensitive matching, i.e., Alabama, alabama, ALAbama, will all return the same result.
* Matching only the first character(s) of the beginning of any word in the item labels to the filter string.

<Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/list-filtering/list-filter-logic.png"
    alt="An example of filter logic."
    contentPosition="top"
    border
    caption="An example of filter logic."
/>

<GuidanceCallout type="positive" customPillText="Best practices">
Increase the minimum number of characters required to filter the list if there are a large number of items and results are slow to load. You could, for example, fetch results on input of the first character but only display them on input of the third. This would improve perceived performance.
</GuidanceCallout>

## No matches

When there are no items matching the filter text, display an explanatory message instead of the list.

  <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/list-filtering/list-filter-no-matches.png"
    alt="An example of no matches in the list."
    contentPosition="top"
    border
    caption="An example of no matches in the list."
  />

## Highlighted characters

When filtering, highlight matching characters in item labels that match the filter criteria. This tells a user why the filter returned a given item.

  <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/list-filtering/list-filtering-combobox.png"
    alt="An example of filtering a list in a combo box."
    contentPosition="top"
    border
    caption="An example of filtering a list in a combo box."
  />

<GuidanceCallout type="positive" customPillText="Best practices">
Make sure that the text in the list that matches the filter string is displayed in `--salt-text-fontweight-strong` font weight.
</GuidanceCallout>

## Loading

When filter matches take longer to return, display a loading message and a [spinner](/salt/components/spinner) in the field. An example is when the system needs to fetch data from a server.

  <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/list-filtering/list-filter-slow-loading.png"
    alt="An example of asynchronous loading."
    contentPosition="top"
    border
    caption="An example of how to communicate to a user that data is loading."
  />

# menu-button.mdx

Source: https://github.com/jpmorganchase/salt-ds/blob/main/site/docs/patterns/menu-button.mdx

title: Menu button
description: "A menu button expands to reveal numerous contextual options when there's limited space to display them. The items within the menu are often less frequently used and don't require constant display within the interface."
layout: DetailPattern
tags:
  - pattern
aliases:
  - /salt/patterns/menu-button
  resources:
    [
      { href: "https://storybook.saltdesignsystem.com/?path=/story/patterns-menu-button--menu-button", label: "Examples" },
    ]
  components: ["Button", "Menu"]

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/menu-button/create.png"
  alt="Menu button"
  border
/>

## When to use

Use a menu button when multiple related actions need to be viewed in context but are not necessarily deemed high enough priority to be displayed on screen. When activated, the menu button reveals a list of actions a user can take. The options are displayed across a single level or multiple hierarchical levels, in a cascading menu. Clicking one option closes the menu and performs the action.

Menu buttons are ideal for where space is limited, or if certain actions are not a priority in impacting the page content. They can be positioned alongside headings, within filter bars, or within alternative layouts composed of various elements. 

## How to build

### Anatomy

A menu button contains:

1. **Main action:** the default action a user can take.
2. **Supplementary actions:** lower priority or alternative actions displayed in a menu. 

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/menu-button/anatomy.png"
  alt="Menu button showing supplementary actions."
  border
/>

<GuidanceCallout type="positive" customPillText="Best practices">
Use a chevron icon to indicate the main action button can expand to reveal options to select from. Optionally, you can use left-aligned descriptive icons to effectively signify a menu item’s purpose.
</GuidanceCallout>

### Layout

- Use a [button](/salt/components/button) as the trigger for the main action. 
- Use a [menu](/salt/components/menu) to display the selection of supplementary actions for users to choose from. 

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/menu-button/layout.png"
  alt="layout"
  border
/>

By default, the action button is aligned to the top left with the menu below. Depending on where the button is positioned within the available space and layout of the interface, the menu will dynamically adjust positions in order for its options to remain visible. 

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/menu-button/position.png"
  alt="layout"
  border
/>

<ImageSwitcher
  images={[
    { src: "/img/patterns/menu-button/screen-space-1.png", alt: "Menu button to the left of the screen with the menu open to the right" },
    { src: "/img/patterns/menu-button/screen-space-2.png", alt: "Menu button to the right of the screen with the menu open to the left" },
  ]}
  label="Change screen space"
/>

## Menu button

Menu button uses a primary button and is used when actions in the menu are related to the core functionality of an application. The button value is typically a string supported by a chevron icon, or can be an icon-only button, provided the icon is well-known and not likely to be misinterpreted. 

<ImageSwitcher
  images={[
    { src: "/img/patterns/menu-button/in-layout.png", alt: "Menu button within a page" },
    { src: "/img/patterns/menu-button/in-layout-open.png", alt: "Open menu button within a page" },
  ]}
  label="Open menu"
/>

<GuidanceCallout type="positive" customPillText="Best practices">
Consider your particular use case, the number and characteristics of menu options you need to display, your layout and available space – when determining the most appropriate button label.
</GuidanceCallout>

## Overflow menu

Overflow menus contain actions that affect a smaller type of content within an interface, such as within cards or data grids. This is typically represented by a three dot icon as the action button. This is useful when space is limited or the interface needs to remain uncluttered to reduce cognitive load. 

<ImageSwitcher
  images={[
    { src: "/img/patterns/menu-button/overflow-menu.png", alt: "Overflow menu button within a page" },
    { src: "/img/patterns/menu-button/overflow-menu-open.png", alt: "Open overflow menu button within a page" },
  ]}
  label="Open overflow menu"
/>

## Icon-only

Icon-only menu buttons can be configured to contextually align to the product requirements, instead of being displayed as a chevron. See guidance for [button options](/salt/components/button) to select the most suitable button affordance for your application. 

<ImageSwitcher
  images={[
    { src: "/img/patterns/menu-button/icon-only.png", alt: "Icon only menu button" },
    { src: "/img/patterns/menu-button/icon-only-open.png", alt: "Open icon only menu button" },
  ]}
  label="Open overflow menu"
/>

## Heading as menu

You can use a menu button to control the content displayed within an application underneath a heading. Vertically align a button to the right of a heading or display text that reflects the hierarchy for your design. Use --spacing-100 between the button and text. 

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/menu-button/heading.png"
  alt="layout"
  border
/>

# metric.mdx

Source: https://github.com/jpmorganchase/salt-ds/blob/main/site/docs/patterns/metric.mdx

title: Metric
description: "A metric displays an important number value prominently. You can add indicators or labels to help provide context to the presented value."
layout: DetailPattern
tags:
  - pattern
aliases:
  - /salt/patterns/metric
  resources:
    [
      { href: "https://storybook.saltdesignsystem.com/?path=/story/patterns-metric--metric", label: "Examples" },
      { href: "https://www.figma.com/file/TI8zR16jnisL4W7ANedtUJ/(WIP)-Metric?type=design&node-id=652-3336&mode=design&t=UpxMBoYUQ8vMxz6z-0", label: "Metric examples", internal: true },
    ]
  components: ["Icon", "Link", "Stack layout", "Text"]

  <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/metric/metric-hero-shot.png"
    alt="Two example metrics displaying positive and negative indicators."
    contentPosition="top"
    border
  />

## When to use

Use the pattern to give more prominence to key measurements. Metrics often serve as building blocks in dashboards. They effectively direct users to key information that they may otherwise overlook, particularly when multiple numerical values are visible.

You can add multiple metrics to your UI if needed. Visual differences, like size and positioning, can help users understand which metrics are most important.

<GuidanceCallout type="positive" customPillText="Best practices">
  - Place metrics higher in your layout when you want to emphasize their importance.
  - Never leave the user guessing how to interpret your metric. Make sure you provide enough context, and use subtitles and indicators to minimize ambiguity.
  - Keep titles and values as short and concise as possible. Round or truncate values to significant figures, and use common abbreviations instead of spelling out words.
  - Avoid displaying more than five metrics in a single dashboard view. This can clutter the user's screen and overwhelm them with too much information.
</GuidanceCallout>

## How to build

### Anatomy

A single metric typically comprises:

1. **Metric value:** can either be numeric or a string.
2. **Subtitles and subvalues:** displays supporting information to improve the user’s understanding of a metric. Subtitles can link to related pages.
3. **Visual indicators:** communicates contextual information.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/metric/metric-anatomy.png"
  alt="Anatomy of metric"
  contentPosition="top"
  border
/>

### Layout

- Use [`Text`](/salt/components/text) to create the metric.
- Use [`Stack Layout`](/salt/components/layouts/stack-layout) to orient a metric in either a vertical or horizontal format.
- [`Icon`](/salt/components/icon) to display visual indicators.
- [`Link`](/salt/components/link) as an action to navigate to additional information or pages from a metric.

<ImageSwitcher
  images={[
    {
      src: "/img/patterns/metric/metric-layout-vertical.png",
      alt: "Metric vertical layout",
    },
    {
      src: "/img/patterns/metric/metric-layout-horizontal.png",
      alt: "Metric horizontal layout",
    },
  ]}
  label="Show horizontal metric"
/>

Metric is available in three sizes—small, medium and large. Change the size of the metric by changing the value text style between display 1, display 2 or display 3.  Metric is available in both horizontal and vertical layouts.

See the vertical and horizontal examples below for individual spacing values.

<GuidanceCallout type="positive" customPillText="Best practices">
 Use the same orientation when displaying multiple metrics within a single view for greater visual consistency. Do not mix vertical and horizontal metrics.
</GuidanceCallout>

### Vertical metric

By default, metrics are arranged vertically with the value positioned beneath the title.

#### Large

  <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/metric/vertical-metric-large.png"
    alt="Example showing large metric with vertical layout."
    contentPosition="top"
    border
  />

#### Medium

  <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/metric/vertical-metric-medium.png"
    alt="Example showing medium metric with vertical layout."
    contentPosition="top"
    border
  />

#### Small

  <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/metric/vertical-metric-small.png"
    alt="Example showing small metric with vertical layout."
    contentPosition="top"
    border
  />

### Horizontal metric

You can display the metric component in a horizontal orientation if that's more suitable for your layout. Ensure the margin height is adjusted in line with the size of the metric.

#### Large

  <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/metric/metric-spacing-large.png"
    alt="Example showing large metric with horizontal layout."
    contentPosition="top"
    border
  />

#### Medium

  <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/metric/metric-spacing-medium.png"
    alt="Example showing medium metric with horizontal layout."
    contentPosition="top"
    border
  />

#### Small

  <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/metric/metric-spacing-small.png"
    alt="Example showing small metric with horizontal layout."
    contentPosition="top"
    border
  />

## Subtitle and subvalue

In addition to the title, you can display a supporting subtitle and/or subvalue within a metric. You can use this to provide more context and improve users' comprehension of a metric's value and its impact.

Place subtitles directly beneath the title, and subvalues beneath the key value.

  <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/metric/subtitle-and-subvalue.png"
    alt="Example showing a metric with a subtitle and subvalue."
    contentPosition="top"
    border
  />

<GuidanceCallout type="positive" customPillText="Best practices">
  To give more context about a metric value, such as whether it is positive or negative, use the subvalue to provide past data, average, threshold or target values, or comparable high or low values.
</GuidanceCallout>

## Link

Display a link in the metric's subtitle text, enabling users to navigate to another page with related information.

Enable users to navigate to another page by linking from the subtitle.

  <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/metric/metric-link.png"
    alt="Example showing a metric with a link."
    contentPosition="top"
    border
  />

## Indicators

Use indicators to provide further contextual information. For example, if the metric value represents a change from a previous value, i.e. from positive to negative, you can display an arrow icon as a strong visual indicator of the direction in change.

  <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/metric/metric-indicators.png"
    alt="Example showing two metrics with positive and negative indicators."
    contentPosition="top"
    border
  />

# navigation.mdx

Source: https://github.com/jpmorganchase/salt-ds/blob/main/site/docs/patterns/navigation.mdx

title: Navigation
description: "A navigation provides users with a structured and intuitive way to go to different pages, sections or features of your website or application. It tells users where they are at all times and ensures they can easily get to where they need to go. Use this pattern to provide consistency that helps users navigate your website or application easily and efficiently."
layout: DetailPattern
tags:
  - pattern
aliases:
  - /salt/patterns/navigation
  resources:
    [
      { href: "https://storybook.saltdesignsystem.com/?path=/story/patterns-navigation--navigation", label: "Examples"},
    ]
  components: ["Navigation item"]
  relatedPatterns: ["Vertical navigation"]

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/navigation/navigation-example.png"
  alt="Example showing combined navigation"
  border
/>

## When to use

Use the pattern to indicate the structure and hierarchy of your site or application content. When deciding on your application’s navigation, it’s important to:

- Display navigation in websites or applications with two or more pages to indicate content hierarchy and help users orient themselves.
- Simplify your hierarchy to help users locate the information they want in the fewest clicks, to reduce the user's cognitive load.
- Label effectively with clear and concise label descriptions or visual cues, such as descriptive icons, to specify the information a navigation item or tab directs users to.

## How to build

Navigation item components are navigational landmarks often used in the top or left areas of the user’s screen. The navigation item component comes in two orientations: horizontal and vertical. Use the orientation that aligns best to your use case.

### Anatomy

Navigation consists of horizontal and vertical variants. You can use them on their own or combined together depending on your navigation structure:

1. **Horizontal navigation**: Consists of navigation items arranged in a horizontal layout, that link the user to a different section of a website or application.
2. **Vertical navigation**: Consists of navigation items and parent navigation items arranged in a vertical layout. Parent navigation items do not direct the user anywhere and, instead, reveals nested navigation items inside it. 

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/navigation/navigation_anatomy.png"
  alt="Anatomy of a navigation."
  border
/>

### Layout

Horizontal navigation uses `StackLayout` with `gap={0}` to display navigation items in a row formation.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/navigation/nav_layout.png"
  alt="Horizontal navigation layout"
  border
/>

For vertical navigation layout guidance, refer to the [vertical navigation pattern](/salt/patterns/vertical-navigation).

## Horizontal navigation

You would normally use a horizontal navigation within an application header, at the top of a page. Use it when you need a navigation that:

- Is always displayed in a prominent and consistent location.
- Affords movement from one set of content to another regardless of where the user is in the website or app.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/navigation/horizontal-nav-behaviour.png"
  alt="Example showing horizontal navigation."
  caption="An example of a horizontal navigation."
  border
/>

<GuidanceCallout type="positive" customPillText="Best practices">
  Use horizontal navigation when you have fewer than eight items. Otherwise,
  consider a vertical group of items.
</GuidanceCallout>

### Default

By default, the navigation item has a horizontal orientation and hugs its content, but you can customize it so that its container can fit any preferred width.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/navigation/horizontal-navigation.png"
  alt="Example showing horizontal navigation"
  caption="An example showing horizontal navigation."
  border
/>

### Using a descriptive icon

You can use icon descriptors to signify effectively the navigation item’s purpose, whether it’s related to a product’s identity, a specific tool, a function or a configuration setting.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/navigation/horizontal-navigation-icons.png"
  alt="Example showing horizontal navigation"
  caption="An example showing horizontal navigation with icons."
  border
/>

<GuidanceCallout type="positive" customPillText="Best practices">
  Ensure that icon descriptors are consistent across all items within the same
  hierarchy level. This helps keep them equally weighted.
</GuidanceCallout>

## Vertical navigation

A common navigation practice is to have the primary categories that represent the main sections of your website or application in a vertical layout, usually placed on the left side of the screen. These primary categories can expand to reveal secondary categories or subcategories when selected, creating a hierarchical structure. It can display many navigation items at once. Use it when:

- You need to show many top-level views.
- You have deep navigation structures.

Read more in the [vertical navigation pattern](/salt/patterns/vertical-navigation).

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/navigation/vertical-nav-behaviour.png"
  alt="A vertical navigation."
  caption="An example showing vertical navigation."
  border
/>

### Fixed navigation pane

Typically, the vertical navigation remains fixed in width when the user resizes the browser. You can set it to the width of your choice. However, you should consider the overall label length, theme, density and screen size you are designing for.

When your application is responsive, the content area should use its own layout grid. As the user adjusts their browser width, the navigation remains fixed until reaching a specified breakpoint, with only the content area adapting responsively based on the viewport.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/navigation/navigation-layout.png"
  alt="Example showing a fixed navigation pane."
  caption="Example showing a fixed navigation pane."
  border
/>

### Responsive navigation pane

You can configure a vertical navigation for fully responsive application experiences. This is useful when you need to reserve more space for the content area, such as for a chart that you want to display in full at as many viewport sizes as possible.

Use the underlying layout grid to set a minimum width for your navigation pane and adjust your content area based on your predefined breakpoints.

<ImageSwitcher
  images={[
    {
      src: "/img/patterns/navigation/responsive-navigation-layout.png",
      alt: "Example showing a responsive navigation",
    },
    {
      src: "/img/patterns/navigation/responsive-navigation-layout-grid.png",
      alt: "Example showing a responsive navigation with grid",
    },
  ]}
  label="Show underlying grid"
  caption="Example showing a responsive navigation."
/>

<GuidanceCallout type="positive" customPillText="Best practices">
- Use a layout grid for the full width of your app’s resolution if it isn't
  responsive, or just for the content area if it is. 
- Use [Salt
  breakpoints](/salt/foundations/responsiveness#breakpoints) to determine how
  the navigation displays at various viewport sizes.
</GuidanceCallout>

## Combined navigation

Combine both horizontal and vertical navigation when users need to:

- Navigate between multiple apps with horizontal navigation, and multiple pages within each app with vertical navigation.
- Navigate other complex hierarchies.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/navigation/combined-nav-behaviour.png"
  alt="Example showing a combined navigation pane."
  caption="Example showing a combined navigation pane."
  border
/>

Combined navigation can be useful in website or application contexts when you want to provide users with a versatile and efficient way to navigate complex content or features. It's ideal when your experience comprises multiple sub-apps, pages or sections, which in turn also require their own navigation.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/navigation/combined-navigation-icons.png"
  alt="Example showing a combined navigation pane."
  caption="Example showing a combined navigation pane with descriptive icons."
  border
/>

:fragment{src="./fragments/feedback.mdx"}

# preferences-dialog.mdx

Source: https://github.com/jpmorganchase/salt-ds/blob/main/site/docs/patterns/preferences-dialog.mdx

title: Preferences dialog
description: "A preferences dialog allows you to display, group and navigate application preferences within a responsive modal dialog window. This pattern introduces guidelines to make the preferences dialog consistent and usable."
layout: DetailPattern
tags:
  - pattern
aliases:
  - /salt/patterns/preferences-dialog
  components: ["Dialog", "Navigation item", "Parent-child layout"]
  relatedPatterns: ["Button bar", "Navigation", "Vertical navigation"]
  resources:
    [
      { href: "https://storybook.saltdesignsystem.com/?path=/story/patterns-preferences-dialog--preferences-dialog", label: "Examples" },
      { href: "https://www.figma.com/file/N6cSYycc4z6XkCjVvc1kIA/Preferences-Dialog-Pattern?type=design&node-id=157-40560&mode=design&t=eq3OapLjaquXm3UP-0", label: "Preferences dialog stickersheet", internal: true },
    ]
 
  <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/preferences-dialog/preferences-dialog.png"
    srcDark="/img/patterns/preferences-dialog/preferences-dialog-dark.png"
    alt="Preferences dialog example"
    border
  />

## When to use

Place any preference settings in your platform or application within a single centralized preferences dialog. These settings could be global, application-wide settings or settings local to a specific window or widget (such as a grid or comments feed). If accessing from a specific window, immediately display the relevant settings when the preferences dialog opens.

We also recommend implementing consistent behavior around applying preferences, whether applying changes immediately or requiring the user to confirm any changes using the button bar actions.

## How to build

### Anatomy

A preferences dialog comprises three key features: 

1. **Content area**: opens over the application content, focusing the user’s attention on a particular task or piece of information.
2. **Navigation**: a list of links that allows users to navigate between distinct panels of content. 
3. **Buttons**: possible actions for users to take. See the [applying preferences](#applying-preferences) section to learn more.
  
  <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/preferences-dialog/preferences-dialog-anatomy.png"
    srcDark="/img/patterns/preferences-dialog/preferences-dialog-anatomy-dark.png"
    alt="Preferences Dialog navigation and content."
    border
  />

### Layout

- Use the [dialog](/salt/components/dialog) components as the base structure of the preferences dialog.
- Use a [navigation item](/salt/components/navigation-item) component to display the left-hand [vertical navigation](./vertical-navigation).
- Use a [button bar](./button-bar) to display any actions at the bottom of the dialog. See the button bar pattern to understand how to implement actionable interactions within dialogs across your applications.
- Use a [parent-child layout](/salt/components/layouts/parent-child-layout) component to position the navigation and content within a preferences dialog. 

<Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/preferences-dialog/preferences-dialog-spacing.png"
    srcDark="/img/patterns/preferences-dialog/preferences-dialog-spacing-dark.png"
    alt="Example showing a preferences dialog's layout construction."
    border
  />

<Callout
  status="success"
  title="Best practices"
>
 - In the parent-child layout, the parent container (containing the navigation) typically remains fixed in width when the user resizes the browser. You can apply an independent layout grid to align the content with the child container. This enables it to adapt responsively based on the viewport size.
 - Limit nesting to no more than two levels, if possible. A deep hierarchy can make it difficult for users to discover or locate specific preferences.

 To implement a responsive experience for preferences dialogs, refer to the layout guidance in the [navigation pattern](./navigation).
</Callout>

## Content area scrolling

We recommend that scrolling affordance should only take effect if content in the parent-child layout exceeds the visible content area.

This is visually indicated by two separator lines above and below the parent-child layout. Apply the shadow-scroll token for the container shadow. 

  <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/preferences-dialog/preferences-dialog-scrolling.png"
    srcDark="/img/patterns/preferences-dialog/preferences-dialog-scrolling-dark.png"
    alt="Example of content section scrolling."
    caption="A preferences dialog with scrolling content area."
    border
  />

Display scrolling affordance when the content or navigation (or both) exceeds the visible area of the parent-child layout.

  <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/preferences-dialog/preferences-dialog-scrolling-overflow.png"
    srcDark="/img/patterns/preferences-dialog/preferences-dialog-scrolling-overflow-dark.png"
    alt="Example of scrolling affordance."
    caption="A preferences dialog with scrollable navigation and content area."
    border
  />

## Applying preferences

Display either a button bar at the bottom of the dialog, or a close button in the top-right. Use the same solution consistently across the dialog.

### Button bar

**Cancel** and **Save** button bar actions allow the user to manually apply preferences in the application. We recommend this when the user wants to:

- Make multiple changes with ease and apply them simultaneously.
- Easily cancel any unwanted changes.
- Change technically complex or performance-intensive preferences.
- Change preferences that can't take immediate effect for any other reason.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/preferences-dialog/preferences-dialog-button-bar.png"
  srcDark="/img/patterns/preferences-dialog/preferences-dialog-button-bar-dark.png"
  alt="Applying preferences."
  caption="This preferences dialog has Cancel and Save actions for applying preferences."
  border
/>

<Callout
  status="success"
  title="Best practices"
>
  Display core actions to the right of a dialog. Refer to the [button bar pattern](./button-bar) for further guidance on how to display user actions within dialogs. 
</Callout>

### Close button

If your preferences dialog does not need a button bar, instead display a close button in the top-right corner of the dialog. This allows the user to close the dialog after editing any preferences. Changes should take effect as soon as the user changes a preference.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/preferences-dialog/preferences-dialog-close-button.png"
  srcDark="/img/patterns/preferences-dialog/preferences-dialog-close-button-dark.png"
  alt="Live updates."
  caption="Updating preferences automatically within a dialog negates the need for a button bar."
  border
/>

## Secondary actions

We recommend configuring the button bar to display secondary actions to the left such as **Import** and **Export** if you need to enable other actions.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/preferences-dialog/preferences-dialog-secondary-action.png"
  srcDark="/img/patterns/preferences-dialog/preferences-dialog-secondary-action-dark.png"
  alt="Secondary actions displayed to the left."
  caption="A preferences dialog with secondary actions displayed to the left."
  border
/>

## Responsive behavior

The preferences dialog is responsive to the width of the application viewport and responds dynamically to the Salt breakpoints. 

Once a preference dialog hits a certain breakpoint, you can configure the layout to either: 

1. Collapse to allow more room for content.
2. Change the orientation to stack the button bar.

### Collapsed navigation

When the navigation collapses, the preferences content spans the entire width of the dialog. To select and view alternative preference types, users should use the back chevron button to navigate back to the vertical navigation. The vertical navigation view also spans the dialog width. A collapsed layout ensures improved usability of dialog content in smaller screen sizes or application resolutions.

  <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/preferences-dialog/preferences-dialog-collapsed-navigation.png"
    srcDark="/img/patterns/preferences-dialog/preferences-dialog-collapsed-navigation-dark.png"
    alt="Collapsed navigation."
    caption="A preferences dialog with a collapsed navigation."
    border
  />

### Stacked button bar

For smaller viewports (i.e. devices with limited screen sizes), it's preferable to configure buttons to stack horizontally at the [XS breakpoint](../foundations/responsiveness#breakpoints). This ensures longer button labels accommodate mobile devices that may not fit within the horizontal layout. They also remain an adequate size for touch interactions.

<Callout
  status="success"
  title="Best practices"
>
  View the [stacked button bar](./button-bar#stacked-button-bar-layout) guidance to understand how to order and build a stacked button bar. 
</Callout>

  <Diagram
    src="/img/patterns/preferences-dialog/preferences-dialog-stacked-button-bar.png"
    srcDark="/img/patterns/preferences-dialog/preferences-dialog-stacked-button-bar-dark.png"
    alt="Stacked button bar."
    caption="A preferences dialog with a stacked button bar."
    border
  />

# search.mdx

Source: https://github.com/jpmorganchase/salt-ds/blob/main/site/docs/patterns/search.mdx

title: Search
description: "The Search pattern offers users an intuitive way to explore content quickly by using keywords. Search is essential to discover information in apps that support large amounts of information. This pattern supports a basic menu driven search behavior, with optional free text behavior and configurable search result items."
layout: DetailPattern
tags:
  - pattern
aliases:
  - /salt/patterns/search
  components: ["Combo box"]

The search pattern delivers a robust and versatile search experience, supporting functionalities such as search history, suggested results, and autocompletion. It accommodates various result types, including search result values, secondary labels, icons, and avatars, offering rich and informative content.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/search/search-pattern-1.png"
  srcDark="/img/patterns/search/search-pattern-1-dark.png"
  alt="Basic search pattern image"
  border
/>

## When to use

Use this pattern to help users
- Locate information in applications with large amounts of data.
- Look through a catalog of items, like a product catalog or a library.
- Navigate to a page or resource.

## How to build

### Anatomy

A search pattern can be present in an application, as a global or focused search, depending of the scope of the search functionality. Independently of how a search is presented, the following elements are present in a search pattern:

1. **Search input field:** A single input field where users type their queries. 
2. **Search icon:** The magnifying glass icon indicates search.
3. **Placeholder text:** Hints to users what information can be searched for. Placeholder text should be clear and tell the user exactly what can be searched for if results are limited. For example, if only page titles can be searched, placeholder text should read “Search page titles.”
4. **Close button:** Close button that appears within the search input field, allowing users to quickly clear their current query and start a new search.
5. **Expand button:** A chevron icon button typically used to indicate that a dropdown menu can be expanded or collapsed.
6. **Section header:** A label used to organize search results into distinct categories within the dropdown list. It helps users quickly identify and navigate different types of results, such as recent searches, suggestions, pages, and people.
7. **Result item:** An individual entry within the search results dropdown. It can include various elements such as secondary labels, icons, or avatars.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/search/search-pattern-2.png"
  srcDark="/img/patterns/search/search-pattern-2-dark.png"
  alt="Search pattern anatomy"
  border
/>

### Layout
- Use [`Combo box`](/salt/components/combo-box) to display search field.
- Use Option Group to group the search results.
- Use Option to display a search result.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/search/search-pattern-3.png"
  srcDark="/img/patterns/search/search-pattern-3-dark.png"
  alt="Search pattern layout"
  border
/>

## Basic menu-driven search

### 1. Initial interaction

Search field displays with "Search" text, inviting the user to begin their search.
<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/search/search-pattern-4.png"
  srcDark="/img/patterns/search/search-pattern-4-dark.png"
  alt="Search pattern layout"
  border
/>

### 2. Activating the search

When the user clicks the search field, a search button appears and a dropdown emerges.

<Diagrams>

<Diagram 
  src="/img/patterns/search/search-pattern-5.png"
  srcDark="/img/patterns/search/search-pattern-5-dark.png"
  alt="Example of search with no history in dropdown"
  border
>

### No history

If there is no history, it displays “No history.”

</Diagram>

<Diagram 
  src="/img/patterns/search/search-pattern-6.png"
  srcDark="/img/patterns/search/search-pattern-6-dark.png"
  alt="Example of search with recent searches in dropdown"
  border
>

### Recent searches

If there are recent searches, a list of past queries appears, providing quick access to previous results.

</Diagram>

</Diagrams>

### 3. Typing the query

As the user types, a close button appears for easy clearing of the input. The dropdown updates in real-time, offering suggestions that match the input, with bolded text for clarity.

<Diagrams>

<Diagram 
  src="/img/patterns/search/search-pattern-7.png"
  srcDark="/img/patterns/search/search-pattern-7-dark.png"
  alt="Example of typing query with no history"

>

### No history

</Diagram>

  src="/img/patterns/search/search-pattern-8.png"

>

### Recent searches

</Diagram>

</Diagrams>

### 4. Direct to the results

Once the user submits a search, they are directed to the results page. The search field remains visible, showing the entered query, ready for new searches.

<Diagrams>

  src="/img/patterns/search/search-pattern-9.png"
  srcDark="/img/patterns/search/search-pattern-9-dark.png"
  alt="Example of direct submission"
  border
>

### Direct submission
Pressing "Enter" after entering a search query will lead the user to the page of the first result in the dropdown.

</Diagram>

  src="/img/patterns/search/search-pattern-10.png"
  srcDark="/img/patterns/search/search-pattern-10-dark.png"
  alt="Example of selecting suggestion"
  border
>

### Selecting suggestion
Choosing a suggestion from the dropdown takes the user directly to the page of the selected result.

</Diagram>

</Diagrams>

## Free text search capability

In addition to returning matching results in the menu, use free text search capability to allow users to enter a custom string to perform a search, returning a search results page with a range of matching results. 

<Diagrams>

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/search/search-pattern-11.png"
  srcDark="/img/patterns/search/search-pattern-11-dark.png"
  alt="Example of direct submission in free text search"
  border
>

### Direct submission
Pressing the "Enter" key initiates the search based on the user's input. 

</Diagram>

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/search/search-pattern-12.png"
  srcDark="/img/patterns/search/search-pattern-12-dark.png"
  alt="Example of selecting suggestion in free text search"
  border
>

### Selecting suggestion
Users can navigate through the menu using arrow keys or click on a result to select from the dropdown. 

</Diagram>

</Diagrams>

### Optional search button

A search button can also be added as an optional element, providing a clear call to action and visual cue, which aligns with user expectations for a more comprehensive search experience.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/search/search-pattern-13.png"
  srcDark="/img/patterns/search/search-pattern-13-dark.png"
  alt="Examples of search when optional search button is on"
  border
/>

## Search result item types
The search pattern currently supports basic search result items that compromise of non-focusable elements: text, icons, country symbols, avatars. 
The following are examples of the types of results items you can create.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/search/search-pattern-14.png"
  srcDark="/img/patterns/search/search-pattern-14-dark.png"
  alt="Image examples of search result item types"
  border
/>

1. **Basic search result:** Displays only the primary search result value, ideal for straightforward results where no additional context is needed.

2. **Search result with icon:** Combines a descriptive icon with the primary search result value, useful for visually differentiating results by category or type.

3. **Basic secondary descriptions:** Adds a secondary label to the search result value, offering additional details or context to clarify the result.
A secondary label can be used to indicate the category the item falls into (ie “Publication”), to tell the type of result the item is (ie “Recent Search”), to give more information about the item (ie “by Author Name”) or some other useful identifiable information.  

4. **Search result with avatar and country symbol:** Displays either an avatar or a country symbol alongside the primary search result value. An avatar is best for person-related results, such as contacts or profiles, providing a visual representation of the individual. A country symbol is ideal for results related to geographical locations or entities associated with specific countries, offering a quick visual cue to identify the country associated with the search result.

5. **Search result with avatar and country symbol with details:** This format combines an avatar or a country symbol with a secondary label alongside the primary search result value. For person-related results, an avatar is used, offering extra information such as contact details. For geographical or country-related results, a country symbol is displayed, providing additional context or information. In both cases, the secondary label enhances the user's understanding by offering relevant details or context associated with the search result.

## Loading results

Indicates that search results are being fetched, typically shown with a spinner used when there is a delay in retrieving results to inform users that processing is ongoing.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/search/search-pattern-15.png"
  srcDark="/img/patterns/search/search-pattern-15-dark.png"
  alt="Example of loading results"
  border
/>

## Search result groups

Organizes search results into clear categories, such as recent searches, suggestions, pages, and people. This structure helps users quickly find and identify relevant information, making navigation easier and more efficient. By grouping results, users can access all necessary information in a straightforward and user-friendly way, effectively managing complex search scenarios. Within these categories, consider ordering items alphabetically, chronologically, or by relevance, depending on what makes the most sense for the content type. This approach helps users quickly identify and navigate to the type of result they are looking for.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/search/search-pattern-16.png"
  srcDark="/img/patterns/search/search-pattern-16-dark.png"
  alt="Example of search result groups"
  border
/>

## Search result order

This section provides guidelines for organizing and prioritizing search results in a dropdown menu.

1. **Relevance first:** Prioritize results based on relevance to the user's query, showing the most closely matching items at the top. Context is determined using user preferences, application section, keyword analysis, and session data, helping tailor results to better match user intent.

2. **Recent searches:** If applicable, display recent searches at the top. This allows users to quickly access queries they've made before.

3. **Suggestions:** Provide suggested search terms or autocomplete options that are closely related to the input string. These can help guide users to popular or common searches.

4. **Data source priority:** If results are pulled from multiple data sources, consider prioritizing sources based on user behavior or business goals. For example, prioritize internal data over external sources if it aligns with user needs.

<Callout title="Large data sets in search results">
The Combo Box has limitations in efficiently handling large numbers of search results. For large data sets, consider methods like limiting the results or directing users to a separate search results page to enhance the user experience. 
For more information, please check this [GitHub ticket](https://github.com/jpmorganchase/salt-ds/issues/4079).
</Callout>

## Search placement

Search is typically located in three key areas for easy access.
<br></br>
**Header:** Accessible from any page, ideal for global search.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/search/search-pattern-17.png"
  srcDark="/img/patterns/search/search-pattern-17-dark.png"
  alt="Example of search is located in header"
/>

**Center:** Prominent on homepages, used when search is a primary function.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/search/search-pattern-18.png"
  srcDark="/img/patterns/search/search-pattern-18-dark.png"
  alt="Example of search is located in center"
/>

**Expandable search:** Starts as an icon button, expanding to a search field or dialog, saving space in minimalist designs.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/search/search-pattern-19.png"
  srcDark="/img/patterns/search/search-pattern-19-dark.png"
  alt="Example of expandable search"
/>

# selectable-card.mdx

Source: https://github.com/jpmorganchase/salt-ds/blob/main/site/docs/patterns/selectable-card.mdx

title: Selectable card
description: "A selectable card allows users to make selections by clicking anywhere within the card. It’s functionally equivalent to a form control, such as [`ToggleButton`](/salt/components/toggle-button), [`RadioButton`](/salt/components/radio-button) or [`Checkbox`](/salt/components/checkbox). You can group selectable cards to support single or multiple selection."
layout: DetailPattern
tags:
  - pattern
aliases:
  - /salt/patterns/selectable-card
  resources:
    [
      { href: "https://storybook.saltdesignsystem.com/?path=/story/patterns-selectable-card--single-selection", label: "Examples" },
    ]
  components: ["Card", "Checkbox", "Radio button", "Stack layout", "Grid layout"]

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/selectable-card/selectable-card-group.png"
  alt="Example showing a series of selectable cards."
  border
/>

## When to use

Use the selectable card pattern when you have options that:
- Are the main focus of your UI (and space permits).
- Benefit from an illustration or explanation.
- Users may need to select on a mobile device, offering a large target/hit area for swift interaction.

<GuidanceCallout type="positive" customPillText="Best practices">
- Consider a more traditional form control, such as [`Switch`](/salt/components/switch), [`RadioButton`](/salt/components/radio-button), [`Checkbox`](/salt/components/checkbox) or [`Dropdown`](/salt/components/dropdown), when you have insufficient space or many options that won’t be visible on screen at the same time.
- Use [`Card`](/salt/components/card) instead if your interactive elements are contained within the card content, such as a button or a link.
- Use [`LinkCard`](/salt/components/card/examples#link-card) instead to navigate users when clicking on the entire card.
</GuidanceCallout>

## How to build

### Anatomy

The following elements are commonly found in a selectable card:

1. **Interactable card**: The whole card is interactive and allows the user to make selections by clicking anywhere on the card.
2. **Image**: Images are optional and should span the full width of the card. Refer to [`Card`](/salt/components/card) documentation for more guidance on using images.
3. **Title**: The title can be accompanied by an optional icon or thumbnail.
4. **Supporting content**: A summary of information related to the card subject. You can use a radio button/checkbox for added visual affordance. Read more on this below.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/selectable-card/selectable-card-anatomy.png"
  alt="Selectable card using a title, an image and radio button."
  border
/>

### Card layout

- Use a stack layout to display the card’s content in a column.
- We recommend using radio buttons or checkboxes for single or multiple selection accordingly.
- Update the padding if you need a small or a large card. Refer to [`Card`](/salt/components/card) documentation for more guidance on custom padding.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/selectable-card/selectable-card-spacing.png"
  alt="Showing spacing tokens applied to a regular size selectable card."
  border
/>

<GuidanceCallout type="positive" customPillText="Best practices">
- Be consistent in your use of images across all selectable cards within a group. Either all contain an image, or none do.
- Keep your cards' titles and descriptions succinct, using similar amounts of text in each card.
- By default, titles and supporting content are left aligned inside the card when using left-to-right languages like English. For text alignment alternatives, refer to the [typography foundation](/salt/foundations/typography).
</GuidanceCallout>

## Single selection

Use radio buttons in selectable cards when your users need to make a single selection from a mutually exclusive set of options. Radio buttons ensure that users can only select one option at a time, preventing conflicting selections.

<ImageSwitcher
  images={[
    {
      src: "/img/patterns/selectable-card/radio-button.png",
      alt: "Mutually exclusive selection."
    },
    {
      src: "/img/patterns/selectable-card/hide-radio-button.png",
      alt: "Mutually exclusive selection without radio button."
    },
  ]}
  label="Hide radio button"
  caption="Selectable cards with radio buttons."
/>

## Multiple selection

Use checkboxes in selectable cards when your users need to make multiple selections from a list of options. Checkboxes allow users to select or deselect multiple items independently.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/selectable-card/checkbox.png"
  alt="Multiple selection."
  border
  caption="Use checkboxes for multiple selection."
/>

<GuidanceCallout type="positive" customPillText="Best practices">
For ADA compliance, we recommend you display form controls. These help visually impaired users understand the selectable options presented to them.
</GuidanceCallout>

## Viewport

Adapt the layout of your cards to fit the size and proportion of the intended user's screen. For smaller screens, you may need to reduce the number of cards per row. For larger screens, you can use the extra space to display more cards.

## Grid layout

Cards are most often arranged using a [grid layout](/salt/components/layouts/grid-layout), which is ideal for larger amounts of screen real estate. Use a grid layout to display a large number of cards in an orderly manner, such as product listings, catalogues or galleries.

<ImageSwitcher
  images={[
    {
      src: "/img/patterns/selectable-card/cards-grid-layout.png",
      alt: "Cards arranged in a grid layout",
    },
    {
      src: "/img/patterns/selectable-card/cards-grid-layout-spacing.png",
      alt: "Cards arranged in a grid layout with spacing",
    },
  ]}
  label="Show spacing"
  caption="Cards arranged in a grid layout."
/>

<GuidanceCallout type="positive" customPillText="Best practices">
- Using a repetitive format or grid layout informs users of the selectability of cards, promoting understanding of their interactive functionality and improving accessibility, 
- Keep cards in your group consistent in height, regardless of where they are positioned, to maintain uniformity.
- Use consistent horizontal and/or vertical spacing between cards to provide adequate touch/click targets, minimizing the risk of accidental taps or misclicks, while ensuring responsive layout across various viewports.
- On larger breakpoints, we recommend setting the gap property to `3` (`--salt-spacing-300`).
</GuidanceCallout>

## Stack layout

Use a [stack layout](/salt/components/layouts/stack-layout) to compose cards vertically and in a single column, to showcase sequential or related content in a list format. This is ideal for interfaces with limited viewport width, such as mobile devices.

<ImageSwitcher
  images={[
    {
      src: "/img/patterns/selectable-card/cards-stack-layout-mobile.png",
      alt: "Cards arranged in a stack layout",
    },
    {
      src: "/img/patterns/selectable-card/cards-stack-layout-mobile-spacing.png",
      alt: "Cards arranged in a stack layout with spacing",
    },
  ]}
  label="Show spacing"
  caption="Cards arranged in a stack layout."
/>

<GuidanceCallout type="positive" customPillText="Best practices">
- For small viewports or mobile, we recommend setting the gap property to `1` (`--salt-spacing-100`).
- Refer to the [spacing foundation](/salt/foundations/spacing) for more guidance on spacing between cards.
</GuidanceCallout>

# split-button.mdx

Source: https://github.com/jpmorganchase/salt-ds/blob/main/site/docs/patterns/split-button.mdx

title: Split button
description: "A split button enables users to perform a main action and access relevant, supplementary actions inside a menu."
layout: DetailPattern
tags:
  - pattern
aliases:
  - /salt/patterns/split-button
  resources:
    [
      { href: "https://storybook.saltdesignsystem.com/?path=/story/patterns-split-button--primary", label: "Examples" },
    ]
  components: ["Button", "Menu", "Segmented Button Group", "Tooltip"]

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/split-button/split-button-hero-shot.png"
  alt="Example showing a split button."
  border
/>

## When to use

Use the pattern for actions with multiple associated commands. Users are able to immediately perform the default action and access supplementary actions, which include more specific or less commonly-used actions.

For example, a paste-focused split button could include: 
- **Default action:** Paste.
- **Supplementary actions:** Keep source formatting, Match destination formatting, Paste text only.

## How to build

### Anatomy

A split button contains:

1. **Main action:** the default action a user can take.
2. **Arrow button:** contains a chevron-down icon and triggers the menu.
3. **Supplementary actions:** lower priority actions displayed in a menu. 

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/split-button/split-button-anatomy.png"
  alt="Split button showing supplementary actions."
  border
/>

### Layout

- Use the segmented button group component as the base structure of the split button.
- Use the chevron-down icon for the menu trigger.
- Use a menu component to display supplementary actions for users to take. Set the component's `placement` prop to "bottom-end" without quotation marks.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/split-button/split-button-layout.png"
  alt="layout"
  border
/>

## Split button affordance

You can use CTA buttons, primary buttons and secondary buttons in a split button pattern. See guidance for [button options](/salt/components/button) to select the most suitable ones for your application.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/split-button/split-button-affordance.png"
  alt="Example showing CTA, Primary and Secondary variants of a split button."
  caption="Example showing CTA, primary and secondary variants of a split button."
  border
/>

<GuidanceCallout type="positive" customPillText="Best practices">
Don’t mix the button variants in the same split button.
</GuidanceCallout>

## Multiple actions

Include multiple main actions if they have the same importance/priority.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/split-button/split-button-multiple-actions.png"
  alt="Multiple actions."
  border
  caption="Example showing two main actions, Copy and Paste, in a split button."
/>

## Icon-only

The main action is represented by an icon-only button to minimize the width of the entire split button.

<Diagram
  src="/img/patterns/split-button/split-button-icon-only.png"
  alt="Icon only."
  border
  caption="Example showing the main action represented by an icon with a tooltip."
/>

<GuidanceCallout type="positive" customPillText="Best practices">
- Avoid using an icon-only split button if your target audience is unlikely to recognize the proposed icons.
- Use a textual label if your main action is high priority. This ensures users are more likely to see it.
- Use a [tooltip](/salt/components/tooltip) to describe or label the action.
</GuidanceCallout>
